utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: Good morning. We will need to sit for shorter periods today. Apparently the witness was experiencing considerable difficulty as the day progressed yesterday with her injured heel. So we will confine sessions to about an hour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: Good morning, Doctor. We will try sitting for shorter periods today to see if it helps with your discomfort. If I could remind you of the affirmation you made at the beginning of your evidence, it still applies. Mr. Borovic.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOROVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Good morning, Your Honours. Good morning to my colleagues from the Prosecution.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOROVIC
utterances.text: The first question. The staff where Dedakovic was, Dedakovic called Jastreb, when did you go there and ask for assistance with Dr. Ivankovic? When was it and where the staff of Mile Dedakovic was located?

utterances.speaker: VESNA BOSANAC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I can't remember the exact date. I think it was in October. At the time, I was attending a meeting with Mr. Dedakovic in the basement of the former municipal building.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOROVIC
utterances.text: Thank you. How many times did you go to the police staff in the course of those three months?

utterances.speaker: VESNA BOSANAC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I can't say with any degree of specificity but more than ten times.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOROVIC
utterances.text: How far was the Main Staff, the staff of Dedakovic, from the hospital?

utterances.speaker: VESNA BOSANAC [Resumed]
utterances.text: About one kilometre.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOROVIC
utterances.text: How far was the police station from the hospital?

utterances.speaker: VESNA BOSANAC [Resumed]
utterances.text: About 200 metres.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOROVIC
utterances.text: Thank you. When asked whether she took the faxes in a car, we heard what the witness replied. My question is as follows: Could the witness explain how this transpired, as she was driving in a car, were there any other cars in the street, how long this took and so on.

utterances.speaker: VESNA BOSANAC [Resumed]
utterances.text: It was quite difficult. The shells were landing everywhere. I would get into a car in front of the hospital. Then I would drive through the street which is now called Zupanjska street. I would pass by the Court and police building. Then I would continue through the downtown area, through the street that was called Bozidara Adzije street, then I would go through Skolska street. I would stop there and go to the -- [No interpretation].

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: The sound was interrupted there twice. I wonder, Doctor, if you could repeat your answer. The sound is still interrupted, it seems.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] May I continue now? Can you hear me now?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: Doctor, we had three interruptions now to the sound. Would you mind repeating your answer?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes, I can repeat it. However, I can't hear the translation of your question now.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: Are you receiving an English translation of my question, Mr. Borovic?

utterances.speaker: MR. BOROVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] No.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: We appear to have a problem with English coming through.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOROVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Okay.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: Okay? It's now through? You can hear the translation, doctor?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes, I can hear it now.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: Thank you. Let's hope we stay on air. Now, perhaps you could back to your question, Mr. Borovic, and we'll try the answer again. If you could put your question, please.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOROVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOROVIC
utterances.text: Therefore, in your daily communication with the staff of the Guards Corps, the witness went there daily in a car. Could she please tell us what was the situation in the streets, how many cars there were, was she the only person driving in a car?

utterances.speaker: VESNA BOSANAC [Resumed]
utterances.text: It was difficult to drive through. The shells kept landing everywhere and one could expect a fallen tree in any part of the road. There were different pieces of debris everywhere, such as bricks and so on. There were still cars in the streets but very few. Mostly one could see the ambulance, fire trucks, and only a few civilian vehicles.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOROVIC
utterances.text: Did she ever use an ambulance visibly marked with a red cross or did she drive in civilian cars?

utterances.speaker: VESNA BOSANAC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Civilian cars.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOROVIC
utterances.text: How many members of the so-called ZNG were there in the three months relevant in this case, ZNG being National Guards Corps?

utterances.speaker: VESNA BOSANAC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I can't give you an exact answer. Do you mean the wounded and the ill?

utterances.speaker: MR. BOROVIC
utterances.text: I mean the wounded, ill, and anybody else who was present at the hospital.

utterances.speaker: VESNA BOSANAC [Resumed]
utterances.text: It's hard for me to give you a specific answer. Based on the information that we have in that period of time, in 1991, there were 3.470 people who were wounded.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOROVIC
utterances.text: Were they all members of the National Guards Corps?

utterances.speaker: VESNA BOSANAC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOROVIC
utterances.text: My question pertained only to them.

utterances.speaker: VESNA BOSANAC [Resumed]
utterances.text: As I have told you it's difficult for me to say that. If you need an accurate and specific answer, I would need to look into the database of the hospital. However, during that time, there were usually 50 to 60 per cent of civilians, members of the ZNG or police members.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOROVIC
utterances.text: So if the total number was around 3.000, 50 per cent of them would be either members of the ZNG or police force?

utterances.speaker: VESNA BOSANAC [Resumed]
utterances.text: It's an estimate, just an estimate.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOROVIC
utterances.text: Thank you. The Crisis Staff, hospitals, who made decisions in the Crisis Staff and who wrote faxes with appeals that the witness described to us?

utterances.speaker: VESNA BOSANAC [Resumed]
utterances.text: The Crisis Staff of the hospital comprised my fellow associates, my colleagues at the hospital, and the faxes with appeals were written by me, solely by me.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOROVIC
utterances.text: Can the witness please explain to the Court why is it that she drew up those faxes by herself without involving other members of the Crisis Staff in the process? Because the purpose of the Crisis Staff is to own sure that everybody takes part in these things.

utterances.speaker: VESNA BOSANAC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I said that I wrote these appeals myself, but upon verifying the information I had at the hospital. Other members of the Crisis Staff had other tasks, such as surgeries, logistics and so on.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOROVIC
utterances.text: Thank you. I'm not interested in that. My question is: Does the witness believe that the hospital was solely targeted by the JNA, in terms of shelling?

utterances.speaker: VESNA BOSANAC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOROVIC
utterances.text: Thank you. My next question is: The Red Cross marks, were they placed on the main building of the hospital where the patients and the witness were or perhaps on some other auxiliary hospital buildings?

utterances.speaker: VESNA BOSANAC [Resumed]
utterances.text: A large Red Cross mark was placed on the current administrative building, where we also had patients in the basement. In addition to that, we also had a large Red Cross mark on the lawn, which is between the old and the new hospital. In the area next to the atomic shelter.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOROVIC
utterances.text: My question is: Why wasn't the Red Cross mark placed on the main building which was the precisely the building where the wounded and the patients were?

utterances.speaker: VESNA BOSANAC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Because the roof on the main building was impossible to access from the outside. That building has five storeys, and when the decision was made to place the Red Cross mark, there was already a lot of shooting going on. It was quite risky, rather, impossible to climb on the roof of the building which had five storeys.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOROVIC
utterances.text: Would you agree that there was no visible mark on the building where you were and where the patients were?

utterances.speaker: VESNA BOSANAC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No. I wouldn't agree with that because immediately next to that building was a very large, very visible, 30 metre long Red Cross sign.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOROVIC
utterances.text: Thank you. How far from that Red Cross sign was the depot, ammunition depot, of the Croatian MUP located?

utterances.speaker: VESNA BOSANAC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I wouldn't be able to say that because I don't know where the police depot or warehouse was.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOROVIC
utterances.text: And you told us that the police station was 200 metres away?

utterances.speaker: VESNA BOSANAC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, 200 metres away. This is where the police station was, where I went to make phone calls and send faxes. I don't know whether the depot or warehouse was there.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOROVIC
utterances.text: My question for the witness is as follows: Was the police building targeted by the artillery or by planes?

utterances.speaker: VESNA BOSANAC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Not only the police building but also the Court building and all other buildings. Not a single building in Vukovar remained intact during the war. They were all targeted. It was just a question of the extent of damage.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOROVIC
utterances.text: I asked you about the police building.

utterances.speaker: VESNA BOSANAC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Like all the other buildings, I said this building was targeted and hit many times.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOROVIC
utterances.text: Which specific missiles were used on the police building?

utterances.speaker: VESNA BOSANAC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't know exactly. It was shelled, bombs were dropped from planes on it but I spent most of in the hospital and I can't say which specific missiles were used on the police building.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOROVIC
utterances.text: My next question and this is something that the witness has already spoken about. She said she spent most of her time in the cellar and the atomic shelter. My question is based on what did she make her assessments as to where the missiles were coming from, given that she was spending most of her time in the hospital basement.

utterances.speaker: VESNA BOSANAC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I never in fact said that I was spending most of my time in the basement or the atomic shelter. My office was on the ground floor. I kept going out. I kept making rounds of the hospital. I would go to the centre of town. I would go home. I would go to the headquarters. I would go to the police building. Therefore I was in a very good position to make an estimate as to how many shells or missiles were landing on the building and the town itself.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOROVIC
utterances.text: Based on this answer, I would conclude that the witness moved about town on a daily basis quite a lot. The question is: How much time did it take when she would go to the police building, when she would go home and return to the hospital, when she went to the headquarters of the National Guards Corps? How much time was she spending outside moving about freely?

utterances.speaker: VESNA BOSANAC [Resumed]
utterances.text: It wasn't exactly moving about freely, because there was continuous shelling and I was always in danger of being hit by a shell. However, I went either to the police building or to the headquarters in order to send faxes from there almost every day. I would go back to a residential neighbourhood, to the residential neighbourhood where I lived, to bring medicine and food there. I would go home to sleep every night and the next morning I would go back to the hospital, although every time I was facing great deal of danger.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOROVIC
utterances.text: Can you tell us how far your home is from the hospital? And did you drive there twice a day, there and back, that is?

utterances.speaker: VESNA BOSANAC [Resumed]
utterances.text: My home is about 500 metres away from the hospital.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOROVIC
utterances.text: How did you go there?

utterances.speaker: VESNA BOSANAC [Resumed]
utterances.text: By car.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOROVIC
utterances.text: And back, right?

utterances.speaker: VESNA BOSANAC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOROVIC
utterances.text: Was your vehicle damaged at any point in time throughout those three months? You must have made the trip at least 200 times in the open without taking into consideration your visits to the police building and the National Guards Corps headquarters. And there were so many shells falling after all?

utterances.speaker: VESNA BOSANAC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, it was damaged on a number of occasions. I remember this one time I was on my way to send a fax, I was inside the police building, meanwhile the vehicle had been hit by a shell. Whenever I drove, nearly every day, it had to be at full throttle. There were no windows or wind screens left on the car. Everything had been shattered by shells, and I could see shells falling all over the place as I drove.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOROVIC
utterances.text: Thank you. On that occasion when your car was hit in the front yard of the police building, did it catch fire? Was it destroyed? Or did you continue to use this vehicle to drive about town?

utterances.speaker: VESNA BOSANAC [Resumed]
utterances.text: It didn't catch fire. It wasn't burned. It wasn't destroyed but I had to walk back to the hospital because at that point I wasn't able to use the car.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOROVIC
utterances.text: So over the next days, how did you go to the headquarters?

utterances.speaker: VESNA BOSANAC [Resumed]
utterances.text: In a different car.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOROVIC
utterances.text: Whose car, what car?

utterances.speaker: VESNA BOSANAC [Resumed]
utterances.text: We had hospital vehicles. The police had allowed us to use some of their vehicles. We borrowed those vehicles, as it were. This was a Yugo and this was the one that I used most often.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOROVIC
utterances.text: Which colour is that car?

utterances.speaker: VESNA BOSANAC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Red.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOROVIC
utterances.text: Can the witness please explain to the Trial Chamber the difference between bombs dropped from a plane and tank missiles? She was after all speaking a great deal about that yesterday during her testimony.

utterances.speaker: VESNA BOSANAC [Resumed]
utterances.text: What do you mean can I explain the difference? Of course I can. You mean in terms of what the explosion --

utterances.speaker: MR. BOROVIC
utterances.text: What the respective missiles look like and, secondly, how could you tell from your vantage point inside the hospital the difference between a bomb dropped by a plane and a tank missile? Is it based on some military experience that the witness has or was it in a different way?

utterances.speaker: VESNA BOSANAC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I have no military experience to speak of, nor had I ever known before the war what a bomb or a shell looked like. However, when a shell landed on the hospital, I saw the way it exploded and I saw the way that a bomb dropped from a plane that weighed about 250 metres [as interpreted] exploded. Two fell at the same time. One fell on the surgery ward in the second floor, and the other failed to explode but rather fell on top of a bed where a patient was lying. I can tell you the difference now because now I'm familiar with the difference between an explosion caused by a multiple rocket launcher, a bomb dropped from a plane or a tank missile. And all these different kinds and varieties of weapons, I think I would still be able to distinguish them today.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOROVIC
utterances.text: I'll ask you about those differences later on. My question is you saw that bomb which pierced through three floors of the building on its way down. We heard about the bomb on the second floor. Was there any other bomb dropped by a plane that pierced the floors of the hospital building or was there this single one that the witness saw?

utterances.speaker: VESNA BOSANAC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I saw at least 20 of those bombs dropped by a plane dropped on the hospital yard, on the hospital surroundings or on the building itself.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOROVIC
utterances.text: Excuse me but my question is did you see any other missiles dropped by a plane like this one --

utterances.speaker: VESNA BOSANAC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOROVIC
utterances.text: But you didn't hear my question, please. That pierced three different floors of the building and remained undamaged. Did you have any other bomb falling through like that that you saw?

utterances.speaker: VESNA BOSANAC [Resumed]
utterances.text: An unexploded one, you mean?

utterances.speaker: MR. BOROVIC
utterances.text: Exploded or unexploded.

utterances.speaker: VESNA BOSANAC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. I told you about the one that exploded. It fell near the atomic shelter, causing the corridor where the patients were to cave in. There was another one that fell on the corridor connecting the two hospital buildings causing the corridor to cave in. It fell on a hospital -- on one of the hospital buildings and totally damaged it. There was one that fell on the paediatric ward. There was another one that fell on the hospital courtyard, and produced a crater that was 3 metres across.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOROVIC
utterances.text: These are three examples. We heard the witness saying that there were between 70 and 80 bombs being dropped by planes on the hospital building itself. Well, it strikes me that your estimate seems rather exaggerated in terms of the numbers mentioned in relation to what you are saying today.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: Mr. Moore?

utterances.speaker: MR. MOORE
utterances.text: I object to that question. My learned friend's observations or his opinions on exaggeration or not plays no part in the evidence.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: Mr. Borovic, what you were doing then was putting your own personal opinion. You've got to put a proposition to the witness, one that is impartial, neutral, objective, rather than your personal opinion. Your personal opinion and that of Mr. Moore and any other counsel is not relevant in these proceedings. It's a matter of the way you framed your question. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOROVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honour, I fully agree with you. You're quite right about this particular part of the question.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOROVIC
utterances.text: My next question: The ambulances that you spoke about, were they burned by phosphorus bombs?

utterances.speaker: VESNA BOSANAC [Resumed]
utterances.text: The building next to which the vehicles were parked and where the workshops were hit by incendiary shells which caused a fire.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOROVIC
utterances.text: I was asking about the Red Cross vehicles. Were they in fact torched by phosphorus bombs or not?

utterances.speaker: VESNA BOSANAC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. They did catch fire. They burned, but I'm not sure if that had been caused by phosphorus bombs. When the shells were dropped, everything caught fire and everything burned down within one -- within the hour.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOROVIC
utterances.text: Are you familiar with photographs that were taken of the Red Cross vehicles where one can clearly see that they were damaged but never burned down?

utterances.speaker: VESNA BOSANAC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I'm not sure which photos you have in mind.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOROVIC
utterances.text: So you don't know. We'll tackle that another time.

utterances.speaker: VESNA BOSANAC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I'm saying I'm not sure which specific ones you're referring to. I have seen a great deal of photos in situations to that.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOROVIC
utterances.text: Did you see the photos of those specific vehicles that we are talking about now?

utterances.speaker: VESNA BOSANAC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I'm not sure which specific ones you have in mind, as I say.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOROVIC
utterances.text: Thank you. About poisonous gases, we heard that bombs containing poisonous gases were dropped. Do you know that such bombs destroy all forms of life, not only humans?

utterances.speaker: VESNA BOSANAC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Based on my modest knowledge, I know that there are several different kinds of poisonous gases.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOROVIC
utterances.text: Based on your modest education, which ones would these have been?

utterances.speaker: VESNA BOSANAC [Resumed]
utterances.text: These were gases that caused tearing in humans, cough, and an unpleasant smell somewhat like DDT.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOROVIC
utterances.text: What do you think about this? When an area was targeted with poisonous gases do you know that this area can't be used for a long time later because it needs to be thoroughly decontaminated before it can be used again and this takes a rather long time, doesn't it?

utterances.speaker: VESNA BOSANAC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, that depends on the poison used.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOROVIC
utterances.text: Thank you. Do you know that members of the ZNG would change into civilian clothes in the hospital in order to avoid arrest by military authorities after the fall of Vukovar?

utterances.speaker: VESNA BOSANAC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I'm not familiar with the fact, at least not the way you're putting it. Most of the people who were in the hospital did not have ZNG uniforms at all.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOROVIC
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOROVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Can the witness please be shown Binazija Kolesar's statement dated the 19th and the 20th of June 1995, page 6, the first six lines? This is a statement that we have forwarded to the Tribunal. The technology does not seem to be fully operational, so we have scanned only the portions that are going to be used and tendered today so we should have it somewhere. I'm not sure if it can be shown. In order to avoid further delays, we have printed copies of the relevant portions too, in addition to what we have already sent to the Tribunal. If you want, I can show the witness the relevant portions immediately so that she can look at them.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: Thank you. That would help.

utterances.speaker: MR. MOORE
utterances.text: Your Honour, may I object to the proposed course?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. Moore?

utterances.speaker: MR. MOORE
utterances.text: I would submit that it is not an appropriate way for a witness to be cross-examined to be shown a witness statement from another witness. I fully accept that it is acceptable procedure to say to a witness, as indeed Your Honour had indicated, "What would you say if other parties had indicated that clothes changed or perhaps referred to the topic, but to actually show the statement of another witness," in my submission, is an unacceptable practice. Because that other witness, witness's statement only relates to that testimony itself, not in relation to this witness. Certainly this witness is entitled to make observations on a proposition but not the statement.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: Mr. Borovic, there is substance in what Mr. Moore puts to me. You will recall yesterday what I said about this. The normal practice would be for you to put questions relying on what you understand to be a statement made by another person who may be a witness in this case or by what you understand may be their evidence. But not usually can you put the statement that you have of that other witness as such, unless some justification emerges from the way the questions you put are answered. So perhaps you could merely pose to the witness whether she would agree with what you believe to be in the statement of this other person. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOROVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you, Your Honour. Well, I'll try using this roundabout route. I accept that there is a rule to that effect.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOROVIC
utterances.text: Mrs. Bosanac, were there people in the hospital who provided security there?

utterances.speaker: VESNA BOSANAC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOROVIC
utterances.text: Was there internal security?

utterances.speaker: VESNA BOSANAC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOROVIC
utterances.text: Done by whom?

utterances.speaker: VESNA BOSANAC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Police members.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOROVIC
utterances.text: How many?

utterances.speaker: VESNA BOSANAC [Resumed]
utterances.text: About three or four.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOROVIC
utterances.text: Where were they located inside the hospital?

utterances.speaker: VESNA BOSANAC [Resumed]
utterances.text: At the entrance.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOROVIC
utterances.text: And no where else?

utterances.speaker: VESNA BOSANAC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOROVIC
utterances.text: Were they armed?

utterances.speaker: VESNA BOSANAC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOROVIC
utterances.text: So what sort of security were they providing?

utterances.speaker: VESNA BOSANAC [Resumed]
utterances.text: They were standing guard in a way. They were just being there. Those inside the hospital were not armed.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOROVIC
utterances.text: And which ones were?

utterances.speaker: VESNA BOSANAC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Those outside the hospital, members of the National Guards Corps, who were in charge of the hospital security.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOROVIC
utterances.text: How many of them were there who were armed?

utterances.speaker: VESNA BOSANAC [Resumed]
utterances.text: That changed. There were always between four and six of them.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOROVIC
utterances.text: And how many inside?

utterances.speaker: VESNA BOSANAC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Three or four police officers.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOROVIC
utterances.text: So a total of, roughly speaking, ten every day?

utterances.speaker: VESNA BOSANAC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I would say it's more like six.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOROVIC
utterances.text: Well, this must be a question of math, then. There were between four and six outside and three or four inside. That doesn't make six. It makes ten?

utterances.speaker: VESNA BOSANAC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, I would round the figure off to about seven but I can't say that it was like that every day. For example, when the shells were falling, there was no one outside. They all took shelter somewhere in one shelter or another.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOROVIC
utterances.text: Where?

utterances.speaker: VESNA BOSANAC [Resumed]
utterances.text: The shelter at the entrance to the hospital -- no, not a shelter. Inside the hospital entrance, the reception area, or in the emergency ward somewhere. They could hide. Of course they couldn't just remain standing out there watching the shells fall.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOROVIC
utterances.text: Thank you. Once the combat activity stopped, what happened to the policemen who were providing security inside the building?

utterances.speaker: VESNA BOSANAC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Some of them remained in the hospital.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOROVIC
utterances.text: In their uniforms?

utterances.speaker: VESNA BOSANAC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOROVIC
utterances.text: What happened? Did they surrender in uniforms, these policemen?

utterances.speaker: VESNA BOSANAC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I can't say. I wouldn't be able to say because I was taken away then. I know that two members of the police force, Lukenda Branko and Tomislav Hegedus never actually wore a uniform, and those who were internal security, they did. They rotated.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOROVIC
utterances.text: You probably made a mistake. Did you mean external security?

utterances.speaker: VESNA BOSANAC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Internal.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOROVIC
utterances.text: You mean internal security had uniforms?

utterances.speaker: VESNA BOSANAC [Resumed]
utterances.text: As I said, two of them did and two of them didn't. I don't know in what state they were when the Yugoslav army arrived. I didn't see that because that morning I had been taken away and I can't remember when they were taken away. I know that some were taken away on the 19th, taken away to be questioned. And the others are still considered missing.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOROVIC
utterances.text: So what happened to the external security? You were outside. This is where you were when the army arrived. What about the members of the ZNG? What about that security? Were they standing there when the JNA arrived?

utterances.speaker: VESNA BOSANAC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOROVIC
utterances.text: Where were they?

utterances.speaker: VESNA BOSANAC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't know.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOROVIC
utterances.text: Did they flee?

utterances.speaker: VESNA BOSANAC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't know. I didn't see.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOROVIC
utterances.text: Do you allow that they might have entered the hospital to hide there?

utterances.speaker: VESNA BOSANAC [Resumed]
utterances.text: That is possible.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOROVIC
utterances.text: Thank you. What would you say if I told you that there were persons employed at the hospital who stated that there were armed members of the Croatian MUP in the hospital, that there was a large number of armed people who were members of the ZNG, and that it was difficult to say who was wounded and who simply pretended to be wounded? How would you interpret this kind of statement and would you agree that it is a truthful statement?

utterances.speaker: VESNA BOSANAC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I couldn't accept it as truthful because I know nothing about that. I know that those who were wounded were indeed wounded. Now, as to whether in those days, when about 1.000 people arrived from the shelters in the vicinity, what was their status, I really couldn't say. I just know that the people who were recorded in our books were indeed wounded.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOROVIC
utterances.text: Did you or any of your doctors ever put bandages or a plaster on a person who wasn't sick?

utterances.speaker: VESNA BOSANAC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOROVIC
utterances.text: Can we please go into private session briefly, please?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: Private session.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOROVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. BOROVIC
utterances.text: Where was this staff located in November of 1991? You said that you went there frequently.

utterances.speaker: VESNA BOSANAC [Resumed]
utterances.text: In the yard of the National Defence Secretariat.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOROVIC
utterances.text: So the meetings were held in the yard or indoors?

utterances.speaker: VESNA BOSANAC [Resumed]
utterances.text: In November, I did not attend the meetings at the Defence Staff of the city of Vukovar. The staff was located in a yard in the atomic shelter. I went there to send faxes, my appeals for help indicating what we needed at the hospital.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOROVIC
utterances.text: Thank you. Do you know Wilhelm Rudolf?

utterances.speaker: VESNA BOSANAC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I know him but not personally.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOROVIC
utterances.text: What can you say to the Court about that person?

utterances.speaker: VESNA BOSANAC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't know whether we have the same person in mind. I know somebody who is called that. I think he is a husband of one of our colleagues who is a dentist.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOROVIC
utterances.text: Yes. You're right. Was the witness ever in the municipal building together with Rudolf, Wilhelm during these bombings?

utterances.speaker: VESNA BOSANAC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Whether I was there? No, I don't remember.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOROVIC
utterances.text: Do you remember ever being with him together in the ZNG Staff?

utterances.speaker: VESNA BOSANAC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't remember. Perhaps he was there but I didn't see him.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOROVIC
utterances.text: What would you say about a statement of the person claiming that on the 17th of November 1991, in -- you attended a meeting of the ZNG Staff and personally proposed that the members of ZNG shed their clothes in order to save them? Is it possible that you proposed something like that?

utterances.speaker: VESNA BOSANAC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No. I didn't.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOROVIC
utterances.text: I apologise. I wasn't specific enough. Did the witness propose that they put on white hospital uniforms?

utterances.speaker: VESNA BOSANAC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No. I didn't.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOROVIC
utterances.text: We heard that the witness saw tank shelling. Would she be able to say to the Court how far those tanks were across the Danube on the other side? We heard yesterday that they were on the other side of the river, on the Serbian side, so how far was that from the hospital?

utterances.speaker: VESNA BOSANAC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, it's hard for me to say how wide the Danube is in that area. The hospital is close to the bank. Perhaps some hundred metres, and I think that the Danube is 200 to 300 metres wide in that area.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOROVIC
utterances.text: So, in total, from the hospital to the tanks, would be how much in your assessment?

utterances.speaker: VESNA BOSANAC [Resumed]
utterances.text: 300 to 400 metres.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOROVIC
utterances.text: This is not a personal question. I'm putting it for professional reasons. Did you wear glasses then?

utterances.speaker: VESNA BOSANAC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. I've always worn them.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOROVIC
utterances.text: What was your prescription then?

utterances.speaker: VESNA BOSANAC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Minus 1.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOROVIC
utterances.text: So at the time, from a distance of 500 metres from the basement of the hospital, were you able to see the tanks on the other bank when there was actually a building between you and the tanks?

utterances.speaker: VESNA BOSANAC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I saw them, naturally I did. Otherwise I wouldn't have said what I said. I drove in the car and I was able to see the other bank where the tanks were.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOROVIC
utterances.text: Very well. We heard from the witness that the roof was set on fire once and that they put the fire out. My question is: What did you use to put the fire out? Who took part in that endeavour? And how many people climbed up to the roof to put the fire out?

utterances.speaker: VESNA BOSANAC [Resumed]
utterances.text: In addition to me, another three people climbed there. The fire was put out with water, and the fire was such that the area between roof tiles and the wall was on fire.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOROVIC
utterances.text: All right. Who else took part in that endeavour with you?

utterances.speaker: VESNA BOSANAC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Marko Mandic.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOROVIC
utterances.text: All right. Did you use the sand that was in the yard of the building and intended for those purposes? It is mandatory to use it in such cases. Do you know that?

utterances.speaker: VESNA BOSANAC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No. We had sand in -- we had sandbags in the windows but we didn't use them. We used water.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOROVIC
utterances.text: If you had sandbags, was that used as a shelter for those who were shooting from there as is typical in combat operations?

utterances.speaker: VESNA BOSANAC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOROVIC
utterances.text: Did you have any sand in the yard?

utterances.speaker: VESNA BOSANAC [Resumed]
utterances.text: What do you mean in the yard?

utterances.speaker: MR. BOROVIC
utterances.text: Did you have large quantities of sand in the yard? Let me be quite specific. Did you have sand heaps with weapons concealed in them?

utterances.speaker: VESNA BOSANAC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: Mr. Borovic, is that a convenient time? We will adjourn now until --

utterances.speaker: MR. BOROVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I was just considering that, that we could perhaps make a break. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: 10.15, we will resume. --- Break taken at 9.54 a.m.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. Borovic.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOROVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOROVIC
utterances.text: My question is: You explained to the Court everything related to the roadblocks and the roads that were cut off. You explained in great detail all the roads that were blocked, how, when and so on. You did that when asked by the Prosecutor. My question is: Based on the great detail that you provided about these roadblocks, I would like to know whether the information you have is of military origin.

utterances.speaker: VESNA BOSANAC [Resumed]
utterances.text: What do you mean?

utterances.speaker: MR. BOROVIC
utterances.text: Did you personally go and tour these roadblocks or did you receive information from somebody in the ZNG or police?

utterances.speaker: VESNA BOSANAC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I received this information from the ambulance drivers, from people who came to the hospital, mostly from the ambulance drivers whom I sent out to provide assistance.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOROVIC
utterances.text: In those days, did you have some military assignment perhaps?

utterances.speaker: VESNA BOSANAC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No. At least I don't know what you have in mind.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOROVIC
utterances.text: What I have in mind is everything surrounding your trips to the ZNG staff, police and so on.

utterances.speaker: VESNA BOSANAC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOROVIC
utterances.text: You said to the Prosecution that you received instructions from the Defence Staff to keep records of the patients and so on.

utterances.speaker: VESNA BOSANAC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOROVIC
utterances.text: Could that be considered a military assignment or a task?

utterances.speaker: VESNA BOSANAC [Resumed]
utterances.text: If you believe that to be a military assignment, then yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOROVIC
utterances.text: Thank you. Did you ever receive information from any members of the ZNG or police that you later on included in your appeals that you sent out with your signature and on the hospital stationery?

utterances.speaker: VESNA BOSANAC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No. I never received any information from them.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOROVIC
utterances.text: When I asked you about the instructions for recording the names of the wounded and so on, my question is when exactly did you receive these instructions, from whom, and where?

utterances.speaker: VESNA BOSANAC [Resumed]
utterances.text: First I received the instruction on keeping records of all wounded persons and persons who were killed. I received that from the main medical staff of the Republic of Croatia in August. They brought us a computer with an installed programme for this type of record-keeping.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOROVIC
utterances.text: And what about the instruction you received from the ZNG staff?

utterances.speaker: VESNA BOSANAC [Resumed]
utterances.text: From the ZNG, I wouldn't be able to say exactly when. It was either in September or October when we received instructions on maintaining special charts called the charts for the wounded.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOROVIC
utterances.text: Thank you. Did you receive the data, data processed in that computer programme and, if so, then where could this data be found?

utterances.speaker: VESNA BOSANAC [Resumed]
utterances.text: On the 6th of November 1991, this data was sent via electronic transmission to the Main Staff, main medical staff of the Republic of Croatia. We still have this data. As for the entire records, medical records and so on, they were taken by the JNA to Belgrade after Vukovar fell.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOROVIC
utterances.text: Am I correct in assuming this is something that the Prosecutor tried to inform us about, namely that upon their arrival in Vukovar, they obtained information that would in future be disclosed to the Defence? Was this perhaps the information that you gave the Prosecutor upon their arrival in Vukovar?

utterances.speaker: VESNA BOSANAC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I'm not sure what information the Prosecutor had in mind. You were asking me about us preserving these records and I told you about that. The original files are in possession of the Yugoslav army.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOROVIC
utterances.text: When my learned friend the Prosecutor was last in Vukovar, did you in fact hand this information over to him or not?

utterances.speaker: VESNA BOSANAC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I gave a lot of information, a lot of files, including the computerised information that we were passing on to Zagreb during the aggression against Vukovar and the hospital.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOROVIC
utterances.text: Thank you. In your call for help dated the 22nd of October 1991, and this is Prosecution Exhibit number 6. If you can perhaps find the document so that you are better able to follow what I'm saying. The appeal reads that on that day, the 22nd of October, soldiers were brought to the hospital, among them Sasa Jovic. Am I quoting the Prosecution exhibit accurately?

utterances.speaker: VESNA BOSANAC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. That's right.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOROVIC
utterances.text: In your statement dated the 19th and 20th of June, and the 21st and 23rd of July 1995, given to the OTP, on page 4 of this statement, for the Trial Chamber to be able to follow, this statement is 2D 01-0084. It was a statement given to an interrogating officer, if that statement can please be shown. This statement reads -- I didn't mean for the appeal to be shown but rather Vesna Bosanac's statement that she gave to the investigators. Is the technology working? The statement, page 4, paragraph 3 of the statement, the statement made by Dr. Vesna Bosanac. Could that page please be displayed on the screen? My question is: Did she give a statement to the investigators on the 19th and 20th of June and 21st and 23rd of July 1995?

utterances.speaker: VESNA BOSANAC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOROVIC
utterances.text: On page 4, paragraph 3 of the statement, which we see on our screens, your statement reads as follows: The Croatian soldiers brought three soldiers in November 1991, which is not consistent with the appeal dated the 22nd of October, the Prosecution Exhibit number 6, that in fact Sasa was brought on the day specified there. So what is true, in fact, the date you gave the Prosecutor or what this statement seems to be implying?

utterances.speaker: VESNA BOSANAC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I must draw counsel's attention to the following fact. In my own copy of my statement that I gave to the Office of the Prosecutor in 1995, in paragraph 2, we see the following text: Up until November 1991.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOROVIC
utterances.text: My apologies, Your Honour, but this is not the same statement?

utterances.speaker: VESNA BOSANAC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I'm reading the statement that I gave.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOROVIC
utterances.text: I only have one statement obtained from the OTP by Vesna Bosanac, and it was disclosed in its entirety. There is only one statement?

utterances.speaker: VESNA BOSANAC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I can show you the statement that I made.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOROVIC
utterances.text: I believe it's a technical error.

utterances.speaker: VESNA BOSANAC [Resumed]
utterances.text: This statement specifies in no uncertain terms "up until November." It may be a mistranslation. However, at that time I wasn't able to specify and that's why I used this wording. "Up until November," which means in the period leading up to the month of November.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOROVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honours the statement that we see on the screen is the self same statement and it has been disclosed.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] My apologies, but I have a different one. The international Tribunal for -- there. Perhaps you have a draft of that statement or something like that.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOROVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] In order to avoid further confusion, it is no draft. There is only one statement.

utterances.speaker: VESNA BOSANAC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, I have the statement. You can have a look and see for yourself.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOROVIC
utterances.text: What page are you on?

utterances.speaker: VESNA BOSANAC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I'm on page 4.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOROVIC
utterances.text: Is that the same statement that we can see on the screen right now, if you could please have a closer look?

utterances.speaker: VESNA BOSANAC [Resumed]
utterances.text: It may be the same statement but it's not the same version. My statement has four paragraphs or passages. Sasa Jovic is in the second one and in your copy it's the third, right?

utterances.speaker: MR. BOROVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honours, in order to avoid wasting time through no fault of my own every single time, because I've been very diligent in complying with your suggestions, but this seems to be a little -- well, maybe the OTP can give us a hand. They are a party to these proceedings, we can ask them. They disclosed these -- this specific statement to the Defence and what I'm asking is, is this the same statement?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: Mr. Moore?

utterances.speaker: MR. MOORE
utterances.text: Yes, well, I work from the English version obviously. It is one statement. There is only one statement. In the English version, I have it at page 4 of 13. I believe that is the page that's being referred to. In the English version, it would be the second paragraph and my translation reads, by November 1991. Now if my learned friend is then moving on to a document which is before the Court and is tab 6, as I call it, therefore it would be Exhibit 6 and page 13, I presume that he's trying to correspond the fact that it is October the 22nd and by November. I know of no other statement and I'm quite sure there is no other statement. But if I could just see the document that the doctor has I may be able to assist. Could I perhaps see that, please?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. MOORE
utterances.text: I'm told actually by my learned friend who sits at my left, one is in Croatian and one is in Serbian. Now, whether that be right or not I don't know. My learned friends would know better than I. I thought they were pretty much the same language but who am I to say? But we have a statement here which goes "do," d-o, [B/C/S spoken] and obviously on the electronic version there is "u." So I think it's the same statement, but perhaps it's the same statement but a modification of the language. I see Mr. Lukic is nodding in a sage-like way in agreement.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. Moore. I think we may have not only the Serbian or B/C/S but we have also a Croatian version. Certainly, in my extremely limited knowledge, B/C/S version and the English version seems to be saying by November 1991. I'm not sure what is in the Croatian version.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOROVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honour, this has been a very nice attempt by the OTP, but despite my warm feelings, I can't quite agree with the way the problem has been put forward. This is a very specific issue. There is a statement that I want to show the witness, it's a statement that she signed in both Croatian and Serbian, the date is November 1991.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: I think we are all in agreement on the date being November 1991, Mr. Borovic. "By November." That's the issue, is it?

utterances.speaker: MR. BOROVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] My apologies. I find it impossible to agree. I'm not attempting to tender this statement into evidence --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: [Previous translation continues] ... correct me. Don't worry about that.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOROVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honour, I apologise for the fact that every time I try to do something like this there seems to be a technical problem but this is not something that I can just walk away from. There is a crucial issue. Just one example, a -- the call for help that I have singled out in an attempt to show the Court that maybe these weren't in fact drafted by the witness. I do have a serious doubt and the dates, there seems to be a discrepancy concerning the dates. On the one hand you have the 22nd of October and on the other hand you have the first of November. And this means a huge difference regarding events repeatedly mentioned in the context of this trial. In the Croatian version signed by the witness it says, "in November," and not "by November." I will leave it to the Chamber to decide which of these two we shall accept as valid.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: Would you -- I would suggest that it would be beneficial if you were to put to the witness the Croatian version of the statement and see whether she agrees with you that it says "in November." Are you in a position to do that at the moment, Mr. Borovic?

utterances.speaker: MR. BOROVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] That is probably the best course of action. Again, I will show the witness the Croatian version, which she also has on the screen in front of her. And it reads --

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] This is a copy that I already have but I want this document displayed here.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOROVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. BOROVIC
utterances.text: Is this your signature?

utterances.speaker: VESNA BOSANAC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I can't see my signature here. It says "signature" and then it's initialed. I can't see my signature on either of these documents, and I can tell you why.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOROVIC
utterances.text: What about the last page?

utterances.speaker: VESNA BOSANAC [Resumed]
utterances.text: One thing at a time, please.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOROVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honour, in the meantime, perhaps I can be of assistance. At the end of that statement, the translator certifies that the statement was orally interpreted from English into Croatian and what I'm showing the witness is in fact a Croatian copy. The matter should really be quite simple.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] These are two different documents. Neither bears my signature. Yours doesn't and mine doesn't. The first document that you have shown me has 15 pages and the document that I was given by the OTP has 13 pages. These documents were used during the Dokmanovic and Milosevic trials, I expect, because the statement was taken as early as 1995. If this is what you wish to discuss, I propose to the Trial Chamber that originals by found of my statements that were signed by hand because these are obviously mere copies and drafts.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOROVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honours, did the witness in fact sign the English or the Croatian version of the statement? Which one was it that the witness signed.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: Or a B/C/S version. Are you able to help us there, doctor?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I need to think back. That was back in 1995, and I believe that I signed the English version. The investigator showed me the statement but the crux of the matter lies in this one word, really. Counsel is trying to prove that my appeal is inaccurate but that can't be proven based on this statement dated 1995, reading "by November" denoting a whole period of time and not one specific day or date. The appeals are very specific about all these things, the ones that I signed at least, when things happened and on what day. That is what I still believe.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: It is your evidence, as I understand it, doctor, that neither of the copies or documents that have been placed in front of you is an original, and neither has been signed by you. You made a statement similar to at least one of them in 1995. Your best recollection is that it was in English and you signed it. You think the two documents before you are different because of their length. Is that the position?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: Now, Mr. Borovic, is it that you have access to originals? I would think not but I ask you.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOROVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honours, all of the documents that I showed to the Trial Chamber and the witness are the copies of what was disclosed to us by the Prosecution. We can see that this is the translated version. We can see it based on this document. However, I have a question for the witness.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: Well, I'm going to just make it clear. If you need the original, we could see if it is available. But you seem to be focusing on what I understand is clearly a translation, and it may be that in the translation there is an error from the original. The question seems to be whether the word used in the original was -- or the phrase was "by November 1991" or "in November 1991" and it may be that the word "by" and the word "in" have suffered some inaccuracy in translation. Now, I leave it to you whether you want to leave the matter there or whether you want to question further on what is before you or whether you want to try and obtain the original.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOROVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I would just like to put a question, one question, to the witness, and I could go along with your instructions to leave that aside.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOROVIC
utterances.text: My question is: In what language did you give a statement?

utterances.speaker: VESNA BOSANAC [Resumed]
utterances.text: In Croatian.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOROVIC
utterances.text: Thank you. Next question: When was there an electrical blackout at the hospital for the first time? And did you in fact have any blackouts?

utterances.speaker: VESNA BOSANAC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Naturally we did. I can't remember when was the first electrical blackout.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOROVIC
utterances.text: How did you manage when there was no electricity? Did you use generators?

utterances.speaker: VESNA BOSANAC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOROVIC
utterances.text: What fuel do the generators use? Is it gasoline or oil?

utterances.speaker: VESNA BOSANAC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOROVIC
utterances.text: How did you acquire the fuel?

utterances.speaker: VESNA BOSANAC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Initially, before the full siege we would go to Vinkovci, to a gas station there, and to -- later on we would go to the city gas stations, and we would also obtain it from private depots.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOROVIC
utterances.text: All right. As we have heard from the witness that she went daily home to sleep there and then in the morning she would come back to work and then go to the police building, to the headquarters and so on, my question is: Did you feel bad about using the fuel that was intended for the generators and for the patients and did you think it was all right for you to travel around in a car and be comfortable while other people had to go without fuel?

utterances.speaker: VESNA BOSANAC [Resumed]
utterances.text: What is your actual question?

utterances.speaker: MR. BOROVIC
utterances.text: My question is: Did you feel bad about being so irresponsible and careless about using the fuel in the way you did and did you feel bad as a doctor going home to sleep every night in order to be comfortable yourself whereas other people had to live in much grave circumstances and you have forbidden other people to leave hospital without a good reason when you yourself did not abide by that rule?

utterances.speaker: VESNA BOSANAC [Resumed]
utterances.text: All right. You're first question: I drove a car which used gasoline, whereas generators were powered by oil. So the fuel was not the same. That was your first question. Your second question: I did not allow people to leave hospital because it was too risky to go outside, in view of the shells and bombs falling everywhere on the hospital, in the vicinity, the entire city. I went home to sleep there during the night, assuming the risk myself, because there were too many wounded and patients at the hospital, and it would not have been humane for me to remain at the hospital to sleep there. So I took the risk knowingly by going home. I went there at night because normally there would be a lull in the evening and there wouldn't be as much shooting.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOROVIC
utterances.text: My next question is: Did other medical staff go home to sleep in their comfortable beds or was it just you?

utterances.speaker: VESNA BOSANAC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No. They didn't. And I have to tell you that those were not comfortable beds. We all slept in the basements in those days, in Vukovar.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOROVIC
utterances.text: All right. My next question is: Can you tell us what a long-range machine-gun looks like? Because there is a weapon that you mentioned.

utterances.speaker: VESNA BOSANAC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't know what it looks like but I can tell you how the bullets look like, the ones that reached the hospital. I heard from the people that those bullets were bullets fired by a long-range machine-gun.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOROVIC
utterances.text: All right. These people that supplied this information to you, were they members of the ZNG or police?

utterances.speaker: VESNA BOSANAC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOROVIC
utterances.text: So they were laymen?

utterances.speaker: VESNA BOSANAC [Resumed]
utterances.text: They were people who were at the hospital. My colleagues, nurses, technicians, drivers, who had some experience having served in the JNA previously.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOROVIC
utterances.text: Next question: VBR or a multi-barrelled rocket launcher is a weapon that you mentioned. How is it that you know that it can fire 16 or 32 shells per minute? Was that something you know on your own or was that information supplied to you by your colleagues, doctors, or members of the ZNG or police?

utterances.speaker: VESNA BOSANAC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I can't remember now who told me that that was a VBR. However, I know how it fires because I saw that and experienced it.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOROVIC
utterances.text: How do you know that -- just a second, please, don't interrupt me. How do you know that it can fire 16 to 32 shells? Who told you that?

utterances.speaker: VESNA BOSANAC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I can't remember.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOROVIC
utterances.text: Before I forget, what kind of electronic communication did you have in 1991? You just mentioned that you had a computer in 1991. So what did you use?

utterances.speaker: VESNA BOSANAC [Resumed]
utterances.text: A computer.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOROVIC
utterances.text: Which one?

utterances.speaker: VESNA BOSANAC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I stated in one of my statements that we received that computer from the main medical staff of the health ministry in August. A technician came from the post office, who was a specialist for that. He turned the computer on and entered data into it. I personally didn't use the computer. I just dictated data. And dictated what kind of supplies we needed, what kind of medical and other supplies. That was one computer that we had. And the other computer was at the headquarters of Jastreb that I also used occasionally when I dictated the data that I wanted to be forwarded elsewhere.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOROVIC
utterances.text: Thank you. Do you know that in 1991, there were no cluster bombs, phosphorus bombs, or Durandal bombs among the ammunition of the JNA, do you know that?

utterances.speaker: VESNA BOSANAC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I have no idea what the JNA had. All I know is what landed on Vukovar and the hospital.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOROVIC
utterances.text: What do cluster bombs look like?

utterances.speaker: VESNA BOSANAC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Based on my information, cluster bombs, at least that's what I heard, are the bombs which do not explode immediately but, rather, upon contact once they enter the ground or once they pierce something, they explode only after several seconds and are quite destructive.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOROVIC
utterances.text: Who told you that?

utterances.speaker: VESNA BOSANAC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't know any more. I forgot who told me that.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOROVIC
utterances.text: That person, did that person tell you that at the hospital?

utterances.speaker: VESNA BOSANAC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOROVIC
utterances.text: Was that person a soldier or a policeman?

utterances.speaker: VESNA BOSANAC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, I don't remember. I don't think so.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOROVIC
utterances.text: So who could it have been? So who could that person have been? A person who had such an extensive military knowledge?

utterances.speaker: VESNA BOSANAC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I can't remember. Truly I can't. But a bomb of that kind fell near the shelter, near the hospital. And this is what prompted us to talk about that and this is how we came to talk about that being a cluster bomb.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOROVIC
utterances.text: All right. My next question: What about a Durandal bomb, do you know what that looks like?

utterances.speaker: VESNA BOSANAC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOROVIC
utterances.text: You don't know, all right. So who told you then that one of the bombs was called Durandal bomb?

utterances.speaker: VESNA BOSANAC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, I don't know. People talked about that. I can't tell you now who and when. But everything that I heard and that I learned I recorded in my statements.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOROVIC
utterances.text: Can we then agree that everything you learned about the type of the ammunition, and so on, was not something you learned from soldiers or policemen but, rather, from civilians in your hospital? Is that what it means?

utterances.speaker: VESNA BOSANAC [Resumed]
utterances.text: It just means that I simply can't remember what I heard and from whom, and as for the effects of this ammunition, this is something that I experienced myself personally.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOROVIC
utterances.text: Thank you. When you gave a statement to investigators, I hope that this bit was accurately recorded. This is all we have in our hands. This is all that was disclosed to us by the Prosecution. I hope that the translators acted bona fide in doing their job. So this same document, D001-0084, page 3, last paragraph, you confirm that this is the statement you gave and that this is the actual document? Could this page be shown to the witness, please? Since she doesn't speak English, could she be shown the Croatian version, please? Or, rather, B/C/S.

utterances.speaker: MR. MOORE
utterances.text: Does my learned friend happen to know the reference for the English translation, please? That would help, if he's going to refer to a Croatian document or whatever so that we can refer to it. Thank you very much.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOROVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I naturally know that there is an English translation, but since this witness doesn't speak English, we have both versions, and the number is 2D 01-0099. Last paragraph on page 3. May I continue?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: We are waiting for the document to come up, Mr. Borovic.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOROVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I hope we have that on our screens, Your Honours, in English and B/C/S. So the witness has the B/C/S version and you have the English one.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOROVIC
utterances.text: In the B/C/S version, I'm saying this for the benefit of the witness, it is stated, line 4 from above, page 3, "the JNA planes dropped on several occasions phosphorus bombs which caused fires that we had to put out. All ambulances in the courtyard were burned down. One girl had serious injuries caused by the phosphorus shell." My question is: Is it true what is stated here in the statement given by Dr. Bosanac to the investigators? Is that true? Or perhaps what she stated yesterday when asked by the Prosecutor, when she said that Silvana Ivankovic was hit not in the yard where the ambulances were but, rather, that she was brought in by the ZNG soldiers, that she had a uniform on her and that she was brought in from somewhere else. What is true?

utterances.speaker: VESNA BOSANAC [Resumed]
utterances.text: What is true is that she was indeed brought in by the ZNG soldiers. You simply misinterpreted this sentence. In this statement given in 1995, I listed there, enumerated there, all of the damage inflicted then in the hospital and elsewhere, and all of the consequences we saw on that occasion. In the continuation of that passage you see that I say there that her uniform was completely burned. We took it off and we put it in a plastic bag in order to preserve it. My statement does not state that she was in the backyard of the hospital.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOROVIC
utterances.text: You are talking here about the phosphorus bomb that burned all of the ambulances, but if this is your interpretation that's fine. We can leave it at that. We will assess later on what is true.

utterances.speaker: VESNA BOSANAC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No. You cannot assess that yourself. I know what is true myself.

utterances.speaker: MR. MOORE
utterances.text: I object to the way my learned friend is cross-examining. I have no problems at all in cross-examination on any topic, but I still haven't seen the English version. I don't know if the Court have got the English version. We do not have the English version here at all --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: Well --

utterances.speaker: MR. MOORE
utterances.text: -- on the screen.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: Three members of the Chamber have it.

utterances.speaker: MR. MOORE
utterances.text: We don't. And I've been trying to follow it on my hard copy. I'm quite sure I've got the right location.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: Page 3 of the English version, the last paragraph.

utterances.speaker: MR. MOORE
utterances.text: Correct. Well, actually --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: Paragraph commencing, "From that time the situation was terrible."

utterances.speaker: MR. MOORE
utterances.text: That is what I have believed it to be but I didn't know if the Court has got, as I say, the English translation. We don't, and I don't know why we haven't. We have got it now.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: Is that the point of your concern, Mr. Moore?

utterances.speaker: MR. MOORE
utterances.text: It's part of my concern because with the utmost respect if my learned friend is going to cross-examine on the point, he has to allow the witness to see all of the documentation that he wishes to compare. I presume that what he is doing is comparing the evidence that the witness gave yesterday with the statement that she has compiled, and in my submission, if the witness is to be given an opportunity to answer, the whole of the relevant passage should be quoted to her. That is my objection.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: Mr. Borovic, I'm afraid I've rather for the moment lost track of what you were putting to the witness because of the distraction of finding the paragraph in the statement. Is it correct that you were comparing what was said by the witness in evidence yesterday with what is in this paragraph of the statement?

utterances.speaker: MR. BOROVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honour, first, if I may perhaps teach my learned colleague a thing, everything, all the documents, have been shown to the witness in both B/C/S and English. I wasn't setting her any traps. Therefore his argument is unfounded. As for my question, it was based on the context of what the witness has read out that I concluded that a phosphorus bomb had fallen in the yard, burnt the vehicles, and that on this occasion the young girl in question was burned. We got the answer that we got. My next question is: At any other point in time, was anyone else who was in the hospital or in the town and part of the official medical record ever hit by a phosphorus shell or bomb, to your knowledge.

utterances.speaker: VESNA BOSANAC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, never.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOROVIC
utterances.text: Thank you. The witness talked about a captain in Negoslavci when she went there for her talks with then Colonel, now General Mrksic. She saw this Captain in Sremska Mitrovica. It's a statement that we heard about. The question is: In which capacity did this captain speak to you when you saw him in Sremska Mitrovica?

utterances.speaker: VESNA BOSANAC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I think this person held the rank of captain. I saw him in the room with Major Sljivancanin, so you have misconstrued my story, my testimony. This person that I met with Major Sljivancanin then I also met later when I was in prison in Sremska Mitrovica.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOROVIC
utterances.text: What capacity, exactly? Please try to be more specific.

utterances.speaker: VESNA BOSANAC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Difficult to say. I wasn't in touch with that person directly in the room in which I was detained in Sremska Mitrovica. Several times on any given day, a number of different officers and persons would walk in and I just happened to see that person too on a number of different occasions but I can't give you the person's name. I was never told what the person's name was.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOROVIC
utterances.text: Just to wrap this up, may I therefore conclude that this person was there in an official capacity, someone who actually worked in the jail?

utterances.speaker: VESNA BOSANAC [Resumed]
utterances.text: My interpretation was that he was indeed there in an official capacity.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOROVIC
utterances.text: Thank you. Next question: Did you see a tank fire a grenade?

utterances.speaker: VESNA BOSANAC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I saw a grenade falling and a tank firing but not that close to me. The tank was firing from the opposite river bank.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOROVIC
utterances.text: But you actually saw a tank fire a grenade or a shell?

utterances.speaker: VESNA BOSANAC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOROVIC
utterances.text: My question is: Now that you have all this military information, would you be able to say if a tank could fire a shell indirectly?

utterances.speaker: VESNA BOSANAC [Resumed]
utterances.text: What do you mean by "indirectly"?

utterances.speaker: MR. BOROVIC
utterances.text: I mean, can a tank fire a shell high up into the air and then over a building, hit a different target? For example, in order to make this as graphic as possible, there is the opposite river bank, the distance is 500 metres, perhaps a kilometre, that's a different question we will deal with that later. There are obstacles in between, buildings, facilities. Can a tank fire a shell over all these buildings in order to target a different facility that is way behind these obstacles?

utterances.speaker: VESNA BOSANAC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I really can't say. I have no military education myself but I saw tanks firing shells and I saw shells falling. Now, what a tank can do over which buildings is not something that I know.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOROVIC
utterances.text: My apologies. I can't give up this line of questioning. You heard them firing and you saw the shells falling. My question is very specific. Does it fly high before it falls or does it fly in a straight line? I'm asking you about this because you have made this enormous effort to become a military expert.

utterances.speaker: VESNA BOSANAC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No. I have not endeavoured to become a military expert. It's a result of my sad experience during the shelling of Vukovar based in 1991. I'm telling you my experience about what I had to go through and you can ask me whatever questions you like.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOROVIC
utterances.text: In order to avoid confusing you, I will try and wrap this up. The shell fly in a straight line or did it fly over various obstacles in order to eventually land in the yard of the hospital? Should be a simple question.

utterances.speaker: VESNA BOSANAC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I saw tanks firing shells. I saw shells falling all over the town. Which tank fired a shell in which direction, whether in a straight line or flying over, I don't know.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOROVIC
utterances.text: Did you see any of the shells coming from high up?

utterances.speaker: VESNA BOSANAC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Not just one, millions of them.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOROVIC
utterances.text: But from high up?

utterances.speaker: VESNA BOSANAC [Resumed]
utterances.text: But I don't know where it was fired from the one that landed in the yard.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOROVIC
utterances.text: A tank shell?

utterances.speaker: VESNA BOSANAC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't know. I can't tell you which type of shell it was. I really have no military education, no military background. I know what it looks like when it falls. I know what shrapnel looks like. There is a lot of that remaining in Vukovar and I can send you one here so you can have a look.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOROVIC
utterances.text: In a number -- in her answers to a number of different questions of the Prosecution, the witness explained that she saw tanks across the Danube firing shells that landed in the yard. My question is whether she saw a shell landing after it was flying high and then falling down but the answer that we heard is not satisfactory. Did she ever in fact see, because she was watching all the time, a tank firing a shell and then the shell flying high and falling down?

utterances.speaker: VESNA BOSANAC [Resumed]
utterances.text: To begin with I never said I was watching all the time. I said this was something I saw. I didn't watch all those tanks all the time, I didn't spend all my time watching tanks, but I saw the shells land and they were landing from all sorts of different directions. From Borovo Selo, from Negoslavci, from the barracks, from all the different sides. The shells were coming in from everywhere. You're trying to suggest that I was watching one particular shell being fired from a tank and then landing in the hospital yard. I wasn't following one particular shell, an isolated example of a shell being fired. I saw the tanks firing, I saw thousands of shells falling. This is something that I saw. This is something that I watched, and you can't prove other wise because that is the simple truth of the matter.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOROVIC
utterances.text: Okay. That's your answer. Let's move on. This might be a good moment to ask the following question: Do you perhaps know what the term "Ustasha" means?

utterances.speaker: VESNA BOSANAC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I'm not sure what you have in mind. I've heard it used a number of times.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOROVIC
utterances.text: When is the first time you heard the term used?

utterances.speaker: VESNA BOSANAC [Resumed]
utterances.text: The first time ever, you mean?

utterances.speaker: MR. BOROVIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: VESNA BOSANAC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I can't remember.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOROVIC
utterances.text: So why are you asking me?

utterances.speaker: VESNA BOSANAC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Do you mean in Vukovar? During the war when I heard the term used or do you mean in general, throughout my life. I heard the term used in films when I was still a child, the term being used, "Ustasha." In Vukovar, the first time I ever heard the term being used in Vukovar was when I was driving that jeep, when I was on my way to Negoslavci, and then a paramilitary person looking much like a Chetnik from films, from World War II, he asked me if I was a Ustasha.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOROVIC
utterances.text: What was your answer?

utterances.speaker: VESNA BOSANAC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I answered nothing.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOROVIC
utterances.text: Does that mean you accepted the fact that you were an Ustasha?

utterances.speaker: VESNA BOSANAC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No. I refused to even talk to him. The young man who was with me Voloder tried to explain that we weren't Ustasha, that we were people from the hospital, that we were on our way to see people from the Red Cross.
