But this person was the sort of person that I categorically refused to even talk to. He was drunk, untidy, filthy. He had a knife, a dagger, tucked into his belt. Not a person that I was able to talk to.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOROVIC
utterances.text: According to information based on your film experience what did Ustasha look like? Did that wear daggers, black uniforms?

utterances.speaker: VESNA BOSANAC [Resumed]
utterances.text: It's difficult. I remember that they had uniforms. They had some caps. I think the letter U was visibly displayed on their led covers.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOROVIC
utterances.text: Were they members of the anti-Hitler coalition during World War II or were they on the same side as Hitler's side, Germany. This is not something you learned at school?

utterances.speaker: VESNA BOSANAC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, maybe I did but I forgot.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOROVIC
utterances.text: Thank you very much for that answer.

utterances.speaker: VESNA BOSANAC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Not at all.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOROVIC
utterances.text: Your husband and your sons, please don't get me wrong, were they members of the National Guards Corps in Vukovar at the time, in the period of time we are talking about?

utterances.speaker: VESNA BOSANAC [Resumed]
utterances.text: My husband was a civilian engineer at the Borovo hospital and he was charged with --

utterances.speaker: MR. BOROVIC
utterances.text: Was he a member of the National Guards Corps?

utterances.speaker: VESNA BOSANAC [Resumed]
utterances.text: You mean at the time in Vukovar? He was in the logistics session of the National Guards Corps.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOROVIC
utterances.text: Were your sons members of the National Guards Corps?

utterances.speaker: VESNA BOSANAC [Resumed]
utterances.text: My eldest son it was a member of the National Guards Corps and my youngest son was only 15 at the time.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOROVIC
utterances.text: Thank you. What about your eldest son? Did he take part in the fighting in Vukovar? Was he involved in combat and when did he leave Vukovar?

utterances.speaker: VESNA BOSANAC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOROVIC
utterances.text: When did he leave Vukovar?

utterances.speaker: VESNA BOSANAC [Resumed]
utterances.text: On the 17th of November.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOROVIC
utterances.text: And when did you manage to get your youngest son to leave Vukovar and how did that come about, since everybody had been advised not to leave?

utterances.speaker: VESNA BOSANAC [Resumed]
utterances.text: He was only 15. Everybody else was too busy and the situation was too dangerous. It was in September that he left Vukovar with his friends.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOROVIC
utterances.text: Thank you. In your appeal dated the 18th of October 1991, or, rather, the 18th of November 1991, it's a Prosecution exhibit. You mentioned that on that day, tanks were targeting the hospital. In your statement, the one that is displayed on the screen, it's the same statement that we keep referring to, I won't show it again. It's page 5 in both English and B/C/S. The statement reads, "On the 17th of November 1991, both the Serbs and the JNA stopped shelling the hospital and its surroundings." Is it correct that you actually made an error in your appeal or did you just provide the OTP with an inaccurate statement? Or did you state that at all?

utterances.speaker: VESNA BOSANAC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, I did. On the 17th, which was a Sunday, there was a lull. However, on the 18th, the next day, the tanks resumed firing. I found this to be very worrying. I still remember that because we were expecting that an evacuation would commence.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOROVIC
utterances.text: What about the tanks on the 18th? Were they targeting the hospital?

utterances.speaker: VESNA BOSANAC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't know if they were targeting the hospital but I saw tanks firing and I saw shells falling on the hospital.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOROVIC
utterances.text: On the hospital?

utterances.speaker: VESNA BOSANAC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOROVIC
utterances.text: On the 18th?

utterances.speaker: VESNA BOSANAC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOROVIC
utterances.text: Over the last 15 years, you never once referred to that except in your appeal whereby I'm trying to show the Court that this appeal is another one of these fake appeals that was sent out to international organisations. Never referring to facts. And that's my conclusion. Would you agree with that, that the fact that you never mentioned shells falling on the 18th prior to this instance?

utterances.speaker: VESNA BOSANAC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I'm repeating on the 17th there had been a lull in the shelling. We were expecting that an evacuation would begin on the 18th. We were preparing our wounded to be taken away. And they resumed firing again, which I found worrying. It wasn't intense firing, there were several shells that landed on the hospital. There was firing. I'm not sure if I refer to the specific date in any of the previous occasions or not.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOROVIC
utterances.text: Thank you. We shall certainly be drawing our own conclusions when the time comes. When you first left the hospital to go to Negoslavci --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: Before it comes a habit in this trial that sort of last observation is not appropriate for any counsel to make. You put your questions. You get your answers. You do not then put your observations on what you may think of the evidence. When it comes to final submissions to this Chamber, you may put your arguments as to what we should make of the evidence or not. Do not put that sort of thing to the witness as you go along. Now, I say that now so that all counsel can absorb that and we cannot, I hope, have to refer to that sort of thing again. Are you going to be much longer in your questioning, Mr. Borovic?

utterances.speaker: MR. BOROVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] That depends on the answers, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: In that case --

utterances.speaker: MR. BOROVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I have three more documents to show.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: -- We will have a break now and resume to a quarter to -- Mr. Moore.

utterances.speaker: MR. MOORE
utterances.text: It's quite simply this. It's to do with witnesses. We have another witness here at the building. I know that there is to be cross-examination continuing and Mr. Lukic, and re-examination. I would have thought that we should therefore take up most of the day. I, of course, am quite happy to keep the witness here. But the witness is, I think, approximately in her sixties and although --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: Quite young.

utterances.speaker: MR. MOORE
utterances.text: And therefore quite young and, consequently, I wonder if it's possible for that witness to be released until Monday?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. Moore.

utterances.speaker: MR. MOORE
utterances.text: Thank you very much.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: We will resume at quarter to 12.00. --- Break taken at 11.23 a.m.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. Borovic?

utterances.speaker: MR. BOROVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOROVIC
utterances.text: Can you describe the officer who took to you see Mrksic in Negoslavci for the first time?

utterances.speaker: VESNA BOSANAC [Resumed]
utterances.text: He wore an olive-drab uniform, a JNA uniform, quite tall, about 180 centimetres, rather dark hair, dark brown, I think, and he must have been 40 to 45 years old.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOROVIC
utterances.text: Thank you. Was he the one who escorted you back?

utterances.speaker: VESNA BOSANAC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOROVIC
utterances.text: What about the next time you went there to Negoslavci?

utterances.speaker: VESNA BOSANAC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOROVIC
utterances.text: When you left the hospital the first time around, did you tell him how to go about organising the hospital security? If so, what exactly did you say?

utterances.speaker: VESNA BOSANAC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I said that we were expecting an evacuation, that had been due the day before. The International Red Cross was supposed to arrive, as well as the European monitors. They were supposed to organise an evacuation, and it was necessary for the hospital to be neutral ground and safe.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOROVIC
utterances.text: Did you in fact see whether he organised the hospital before you left or not? Did he organise security for the hospital and only then were you in fact on your way?

utterances.speaker: VESNA BOSANAC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOROVIC
utterances.text: How exactly did that work? How many soldiers did he organise and who did he give orders to?

utterances.speaker: VESNA BOSANAC [Resumed]
utterances.text: He gave orders to a soldier who was supposed to carry it out. He said that two soldiers should guard each of the hospital's entrances. Later on, upon my return, I saw two soldiers standing at the entrance that I used on my way in.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOROVIC
utterances.text: And you supposed that there were other soldiers in front of other entrances?

utterances.speaker: VESNA BOSANAC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. I suppose so.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOROVIC
utterances.text: On your way back from Negoslavci, as you told us, upon your request, the soldiers stopped the vehicle and your mother came in?

utterances.speaker: VESNA BOSANAC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOROVIC
utterances.text: Upon your request, were the soldiers able to find your parents in law?

utterances.speaker: VESNA BOSANAC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOROVIC
utterances.text: Upon your request on that day, did Mrksic comply with your request and were there food supplies awaiting you at the hospital upon your return?

utterances.speaker: VESNA BOSANAC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOROVIC
utterances.text: Did they know that you were Vesna Bosanac?

utterances.speaker: VESNA BOSANAC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. I introduced myself.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOROVIC
utterances.text: When you asked them to pick up your mother and to go look for your parents in law, did they know that you were Vesna Bosanac, director of the hospital?

utterances.speaker: VESNA BOSANAC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOROVIC
utterances.text: Based on the reports of the international observers, do you know how many people were transported in a convoy that was supposed to be evacuated on that day?

utterances.speaker: VESNA BOSANAC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't know.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOROVIC
utterances.text: On the 19th of November, how many wounded and ill there were at the hospital?

utterances.speaker: VESNA BOSANAC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Between 400 and 450.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOROVIC
utterances.text: All right. If in Ovcara regrettably so many people lost their lives, and if based on the reports of international observers, over 400 people were evacuated, does that mean that there should have been 800 wounded at the hospital who should have been evacuated or not?

utterances.speaker: VESNA BOSANAC [Resumed]
utterances.text: As I said, there were about 400 ill and wounded patients.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOROVIC
utterances.text: All right.

utterances.speaker: VESNA BOSANAC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Please allow me to complete my answer. Based on all reports, 174 wounded were evacuated, 120 on the first day, the 20th of November, and another 54 on the second day. So a total of 174 wounded persons were transported to Croatia. Please allow me to finish. Out of 200 exhumed bodies, exhumed from the mass grave in Ovcara, based on our reports, 97 of them were wounded.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOROVIC
utterances.text: All right. We will deal with that on another occasion. I'm not interested in that. Based on the information you had then, and today, were you able to conclude who was the person in charge, representing the JNA in charge of the evacuation?

utterances.speaker: VESNA BOSANAC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I can say that up until the 19th, I believed that it was General Raseta who signed the agreement. I believed him to be in charge of the evacuation. On the 19th, when I was in Negoslavci, Colonel Mrksic told me that only Raseta -- that Raseta can sign and negotiate anything he wanted, but that Raseta was not there on the ground and that it was him who was going to organise the evacuation. And then, on the 20th of November, ultimately, the then Major Sljivancanin organised the evacuation of the hospital.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOROVIC
utterances.text: Do you know what role Nebojsa Pavkovic, the general, played?

utterances.speaker: VESNA BOSANAC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOROVIC
utterances.text: You don't know, all right. Do you know Nestorovic, Ivica, the JNA soldier from Zranjanin [phoen]? Have you heard of him?

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Could the witness please repeat the answer?

utterances.speaker: MR. BOROVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. BOROVIC
utterances.text: Did you know where the warehouse of Borovo Komerc was located at the time?

utterances.speaker: VESNA BOSANAC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I heard that name for the first time in prison when I was interrogated.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOROVIC
utterances.text: I asked you about the Borovo Komerc warehouse.

utterances.speaker: VESNA BOSANAC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I naturally knew where it was located. The basement of that company was turned into a shelter. We sent the wounded there after treating them at the hospital.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOROVIC
utterances.text: Do you know how many wounded were there?

utterances.speaker: VESNA BOSANAC [Resumed]
utterances.text: According to my information, there were about 200 wounded there before the Priljevo locality was blocked off. I spoke to the then Colonel Mrksic about it, and after the evacuation of the hospital, there was supposed to be an evacuation of the people from Borovo Komerc.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOROVIC
utterances.text: Did you take part in that evacuation in Borovo Komerc?

utterances.speaker: VESNA BOSANAC [Resumed]
utterances.text: The people who were tasked with that location did that.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOROVIC
utterances.text: And those were?

utterances.speaker: VESNA BOSANAC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Kuzmanovic, Djordje, Ramik [phoen], Vladimir, and Simonovic, Zlatko. They were all physicians.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOROVIC
utterances.text: Did you know Dr. Kuzmanovic, Djordje, personally?

utterances.speaker: VESNA BOSANAC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOROVIC
utterances.text: Did you ever receive the records of the wounded and the injured in Borovo Komerc?

utterances.speaker: VESNA BOSANAC [Resumed]
utterances.text: We only discussed the number of people, their needs, on the phone.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOROVIC
utterances.text: Was that recorded somewhere after the telephone conversation?

utterances.speaker: VESNA BOSANAC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. We recorded all that. We recorded how much was sent or rather how many people were sent there twice a week or on a daily basis, and then we also recorded how many people were sent elsewhere once that location was full.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOROVIC
utterances.text: Was that information on the wounded and the injured from Borovo Komerc entered into your computer database?

utterances.speaker: VESNA BOSANAC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOROVIC
utterances.text: Why not?

utterances.speaker: VESNA BOSANAC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Because while we were entering the data, people were entered into the computer database when there were wounded and that was done at the hospital. Once they were sent elsewhere it Borovo Komerc they would occasionally come back to be bandaged or provided some further treatment.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOROVIC
utterances.text: Your husband, who was the director of the warehouse in Borovo Komerc, was he involved in that?

utterances.speaker: VESNA BOSANAC [Resumed]
utterances.text: He was at that location. What period of time do you have in mind?

utterances.speaker: MR. BOROVIC
utterances.text: War time.

utterances.speaker: VESNA BOSANAC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. During war time he was there. He was at Borovo Komerc.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOROVIC
utterances.text: Did he have contact with the wounded persons?

utterances.speaker: VESNA BOSANAC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. He had contact both with the wounded, the ill, and the doctors.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOROVIC
utterances.text: What was his role in that period of time?

utterances.speaker: VESNA BOSANAC [Resumed]
utterances.text: You mean my husband?

utterances.speaker: MR. BOROVIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: VESNA BOSANAC [Resumed]
utterances.text: In the Borovo Komerc warehouse, they organised logistical support, meaning electricity and water supply, bread-baking, then building coffins for burying the dead and so on.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOROVIC
utterances.text: In that Borovo Komerc warehouse, were there any members of police or National Guards Corps?

utterances.speaker: VESNA BOSANAC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOROVIC
utterances.text: How many?

utterances.speaker: VESNA BOSANAC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't know exactly.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOROVIC
utterances.text: All right. Do you know Dr. Kovacic?

utterances.speaker: VESNA BOSANAC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOROVIC
utterances.text: Were you ever called from the Borovo Komerc warehouse asking you to treat somebody medically or not?

utterances.speaker: VESNA BOSANAC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I stated in my testimony that all of the wounded were first brought to the hospital because this is where we had operation rooms and surgeons. When the Priljevo road fell, I don't know exactly whether it was, but sometime in early November, then the wounded, the gravely wounded, were first brought to the hospital. Later on, upon my return from prison, I heard that they admitted and treated the wounded in Borovo Naselje, those who were unable to reach the hospital.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOROVIC
utterances.text: All right. Did you personally ever operate on a Serb?

utterances.speaker: VESNA BOSANAC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Who? I? No, I'm not a surgeon.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOROVIC
utterances.text: I'm just asking. Anybody can be a surgeon during wartime?

utterances.speaker: VESNA BOSANAC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, never. Only qualified surgeons operated in our hospital.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOROVIC
utterances.text: Would you have done that? Would you have operated on a Serb if you had an occasion?

utterances.speaker: VESNA BOSANAC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I would do it only if I was the only doctor and there were no surgeons anywhere around.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOROVIC
utterances.text: Is it likely that you would have done that or would you have definitely done it?

utterances.speaker: VESNA BOSANAC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, depending on the circumstances. In exceptional circumstances, if I were the only doctor, and it was an emergency, yes, I would do that regardless of whether the patient was a Serb or a Croat, because the patient is first and foremost a patient, and I have to analyse the situation.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOROVIC
utterances.text: All right. Now a more important question: Was there ever a decision issued to commence investigation against you for committing a war crime?

utterances.speaker: VESNA BOSANAC [Resumed]
utterances.text: As far as I know, it wasn't.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOROVIC
utterances.text: Do you know whether proceedings were ever instituted against you for a war crime?

utterances.speaker: VESNA BOSANAC [Resumed]
utterances.text: As far as I know, no.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOROVIC
utterances.text: Did you give a statement to the military court in Belgrade in relation to any criminal proceedings?

utterances.speaker: VESNA BOSANAC [Resumed]
utterances.text: After I wrote the statement in Sremska Mitrovica, the one we discussed, I was taken, as far as I could tell, to the military investigative prison in Belgrade, where I was subjected to interrogation. I don't know what the charges against me were. I know that they interrogated me about why I wrote something against the JNA. At the time, I still had some original faxes with me, and if this is what you have in mind, yes, I did have a counsel assigned to me and the interrogation lasted, I don't know for how many hours, perhaps a day. This Court appointed counsel told me that he didn't think I would be indicted in the end because pursuant to the then military regulations, there was no verbal offence, and that was just prior to my being exchanged and sent in the military plane to Belgrade.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOROVIC
utterances.text: My next question: Were you exchanged in accordance with the principle all for all?

utterances.speaker: VESNA BOSANAC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't know how I was exchanged. I know that I was in a group with another 44 persons. On that day we were first brought to the military investigative prison in Belgrade, and then after two days we were taken to an airport and transferred to Zagreb in two planes.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOROVIC
utterances.text: My question is -- my next question is: The plane that transported you to Zagreb, was General Aca Vasiljevic on that plane?

utterances.speaker: VESNA BOSANAC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No. He was in the other plane.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOROVIC
utterances.text: All right. Does that mean that all of you who came to the military court in Belgrade were exchanged?

utterances.speaker: VESNA BOSANAC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't know who was in the military court then, but I know that it was all of us who were on that bus, all of us were exchanged.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOROVIC
utterances.text: And how many people were there?

utterances.speaker: VESNA BOSANAC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, I know that two people decided not to be exchanged and that there was a total of 45 of us.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOROVIC
utterances.text: All right.

utterances.speaker: VESNA BOSANAC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I'm not sure.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOROVIC
utterances.text: Some of the people were acquitted by the military court so they never had to be exchanged. Do you know that?

utterances.speaker: VESNA BOSANAC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't know. I don't know what they were charged with.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOROVIC
utterances.text: Well, I'll give you some details. Soldier Vukas who was tried by Colonel Milicevic was acquitted. Do you know that?

utterances.speaker: VESNA BOSANAC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, I don't.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOROVIC
utterances.text: All right. You would probably be surprised if you were to hear who defence counsel was?

utterances.speaker: MR. MOORE
utterances.text: I object to this question. I submit it has no obvious relevance to the issue to be determined by the Court.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: Mr. Borovic, is there a relevance that you can offer?

utterances.speaker: MR. BOROVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] You mean my last question?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: Yes. And this line of questioning now about acquittals.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOROVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I naturally could explain the relevance to you, but I will not proceed with it. Everything that I'm putting to the witness related to the military court will be tendered into evidence by me at the end of the cross-examination. My next question for the witness is --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: [Previous translation continues] ... demonstrate then that it is relevant? So think about it and be ready with that. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOROVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I'm quite prepared, and hence my next question.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOROVIC
utterances.text: Did the American embassy provide any support for exchanging Vesna Bosanac?

utterances.speaker: VESNA BOSANAC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't know that.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOROVIC
utterances.text: Do you know that persons responsible for committing a war crime in accordance with all international conventions may not be exchanged?

utterances.speaker: VESNA BOSANAC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I'm not aware of that.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOROVIC
utterances.text: I would like tab 2 to be tendered into evidence, tab 2, tab 3 and tab 4. The number is 12-2 D 01-5. The next one is 13-2 D 01-007. And the last one is tab 4 and the number is 14-2 D 01-0010. The documents are information by the first department of the 1st Military District, taken from Djordje Kuzmanovic, a physician, that the witness spoke about today. The next thing we have is an official note?

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Excuse me, could you just please read out again the numbers you would like -- of the documents that you would like us to present, the ID numbers, please?

utterances.speaker: MR. BOROVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Tab 1, number 12-2 D 01-0005. Tab 13, number 13-2 D 01-007. Finally, 14-2 D 01-0010. Is that all right now?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: When you referred to tabs, were you referring to the small bundle of four documents that you provided earlier?

utterances.speaker: MR. BOROVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Precisely so, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: It's tabs 2, 3, and 4; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: MR. BOROVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes. But pursuant to instructions we received from the Registrar, we read them out this way, tabs 1, 2, 3, and 4. Finally, Your Honour --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: We are still looking at this issue. The first of those is the document concerning Kuzmanovic. That's a document alleging conduct concerning a private, Nestorovic, and his medical treatment. Is that the one? Now, do you say that the witness has knowledge of this document or are you simply seeking to tender it on the basis that it is a document which on its face is authenticated and has some relevance to the case?

utterances.speaker: MR. BOROVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honour, the documents from tab 2 and tab 3 are part and parcel of the document under tab 4, which is a decision to commence investigation. The witness may not necessarily be familiar with the first two documents but she must be familiar with the request for an investigation to be conducted because she did say a while ago that she was questioned at the military court. This is 19/12 -- -12/92 from 1992. I believe them to be relevant in every way because there is reference to Dr. Kuzmanovic, someone the witness is familiar with. He is a source of information based on which the military Prosecutor filed a request to institute an investigation.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: As I understood the evidence of Dr. Bosanac, while she appreciated she was being questioned, she said she did not know that she had been the subject of a formal order for investigation. Is that correct, doctor? Have you seen --

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: -- a document that formally orders there to be an investigation into aspects of your conduct?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] No.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOROVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honour?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOROVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] By the Chamber's leave according to the law of criminal procedure of the Social Federal Republic of Yugoslavia, in order for someone to give a statement, there has to be a request first to carry out an investigation. In order for someone to declare their position, they have to have counsel assigned. We heard that an attorney was in fact assigned ex officio. If this is an informal interview, there is no counsel involved. Based on what the witness has told us herself, based on the documents in the files of the military court, this was the only place where she could possibly have given a statement. The statement was not given in the military police building. It was given at the military court on military court premises. It definitely is relevant. She is free to say that she is not familiar with this. She is free to say that she has no idea of ever being accused of committing a war crime, but it's up to me to investigate the matter further and to ask questions in relation to it.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: Mr. Borovic, I do not at the moment have any basis for doubting that these orders existed or were made. The witness, though, says she knew nothing of them at the time. Mr. More, is there any objection to the tendering first for the order for investigation?

utterances.speaker: MR. MOORE
utterances.text: Yes. The documents in our submission really should be subdivided into two specific categories. May I deal with the investigation document? If we take by way of analogy and will he us say we have Mr. Radic who is giving evidence, I ask him a question, "Do you know the name of Madam Carla Del Ponte?", and he says "Yes." And I then attempt to adduce in evidence a report compiled by her suggesting that an investigation should proceed and itemising or particularising what the belief is, in my submission, that would be a wholly inappropriate course because it is of no relevance to the issue to be determined by the Court. It is merely a document which suggests that an investigation should proceed. There are two different issues here. One is the knowledge of the investigation, and two, whether in fact there is an awareness of the content of the document. And they should be subdivided. They cannot be mixed. So that would be my first objection. This is merely a document saying, commence investigation. The witness should be asked, are you aware that you were under investigation? The answer can either be yes or no but it bears no --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: She has been asked. She says she was not aware of a formal investigation but she certainly was aware that she was questioned. And that a counsel was assigned.

utterances.speaker: MR. MOORE
utterances.text: Yes. I have no dispute and I take no point on that and took no point but this is different. This is the actual document itself that gives the parameters of the investigation. And the doctor has said already that she was not aware of that existence or the existence of this document. Therefore, in my submission, it is an inadmissible document. Because there is no relevance to her. She does not know the document itself, merely the fact she was being investigated.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: You sound to be echoing good old fashioned common law rules rather than the procedure of this Tribunal, Mr. Moore.

utterances.speaker: MR. MOORE
utterances.text: Well, I probably --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: A document which on its face has apparent relevance may be admitted here, whether it's of any weight or use being determined later.

utterances.speaker: MR. MOORE
utterances.text: I am aware that I argue common law rules, perhaps more than civil rules. However, the test --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: These are not the Rules of this Tribunal.

utterances.speaker: MR. MOORE
utterances.text: Yes, but the test that must apply is the test of relevance, vis-a-vis the witness or an issue to be determined by the Court.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: Can I pose as a possible relevance that the witness says she was taken to a military prison where she was questioned and a counsel was assigned, either one possible view is that was an entirely illegal and outrageous procedure and shows the way that she was badly treated. The other view is that it was conducted in accordance with the law prevailing at the time and these documents establish that so that even though the witness may not have known in fact that the lawful procedure was being followed.

utterances.speaker: MR. MOORE
utterances.text: Well, one must try and ascertain to which issue this document is driven. In my submission, the test has, as I say, be relevance to either an issue to be determined before the Court, or within the scope of the knowledge of the witness. Now, if the witness says no, I do not know this, clearly, if there is a document in existence which may state, well, this is wrong, clearly this is a situation where there was a counsel or there was a procedure adopted, I would query whether in actual fact the document should be admitted at this stage in any event. But I equally submit that one has to look at the purpose of the document itself and why it's being advanced. She has said I do not know of this document. If that is the case, irrespective of whether it be civil or common law rules, in my submission it is not a document that can come before the Court at this stage. It may well be that the Defence in due course will be able to call evidence to deal with this issue. It may well be it can be done in a formal way in the Defence case. To say quite simply it has been said in evidence by Dr. Bosanac that she was not -- and then particularising A, B, C, D. Now, do you happen to have any documents which deal with this issue? And it may well be that there is someone from the judiciary or an investigator who can demonstrate evidentially documentation that would put the sore to Dr. Bosanac's evidence. But at this stage, it is inappropriate and in my submission, whether it be common law or civil jurisdiction, that is the way that it should be done.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: The other two documents, Mr. Moore.

utterances.speaker: MR. MOORE
utterances.text: The other two documents? We have only really dealt with one so far but I can deal with the other. If we deal with the report from the 1st Military District command, it appears the 2nd of December 1991, and it seems to be a conclusion in relation to behaviour on the 13th of November in respect of an incident at a warehouse. We would submit it bears absolutely no relevance to Dr. Bosanac's evidence at all. It relates to a different area. It relates to the 13th of November. There is nothing to suggest that she participated in this and we equally submit that the document itself is merely a finding, if it be a finding, in relation to an irrelevant issue and, as such, can only be admissible if it can be shown to be linked to this doctor. Now, let me give a small example, if I may. If, for example, there was evidence before the Court to show that Dr. Bosanac was actually existing at this location at this time, was responsible for not only medical treatment but surgical treatment, it may well be then argued, well, You say that you do not do operations, or perhaps you could say, Do do operations, but here we would suggest is an incident on the 13th of November where it is said that this individual received no medical treatment. I want to ask you the following questions. Firstly, are you aware of this individual? Secondly, were you on duty at that time? Thirdly, were you responsible for the operations that were to participate or be participated in at that time? And if you were, how do you explain the fact that this person received no medical treatment? The conclusion of another party in my submission bears no relevance to Dr. Bosanac's evidence. And there is no nexus to link it. With regard to the second document, which I see is dated the 25th of November, officially secret, strictly confidential, I'm not quite sure exactly the purpose of this document. It hasn't been dealt with, as far as I'm aware. It is merely an apparent finding. If that is the case, the appropriate time for this evidence to be given is at the defence stage so the Prosecution have an opportunity to cross-examine the witness. As I say, I don't know exactly what the purpose of this document is because we have not heard as yet.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. Moore. Mr. Borovic, as you heard, there is an objection made to the reception of all three documents. Now, if you wish to pursue them, could you first of all explain to the Chamber the relevance to the issues in this case of the document which is the order for military investigation? That's if you want to pursue its admission.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOROVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honour, that is of course what I intend to do. My learned friend has used a lot of sentences, a lot of words. My experience tells me that this is usually what you do when you face an absence of arguments. I'm not even sure where we first began although my power of focusing is usually great.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: Can I try and assist you, then, to focus? I want you to tell me what in your case is the relevance of this document.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOROVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I am in fact very focused. I don't think I require any assistance in that respect. My first question to Vesna Bosanac was, Does she know Ivica Nestorevic. Now this is the initial fact that I inquired about. The next was, Does she know about Borovo Naselje, the neighbourhood, the third fact, that the fact that the Vukovar medical centre was in charge, which is something this we know from her previous testimony. Fact number 4, they register the wounded and ill from Borovo Kladista [phoen] upon their admittance. Fact number 5, indeed highly relevant, we do not have an alleged conclusion or a finding. We have a court decision ruling to commence investigation. Vesna Bosanac, the witness, never challenged the fact that she gave a statement to the military investigator. My question was -- I even have a transcript which deliberately I will not be showing now. She signed it and this would be too early a point to show it, in our strategy. There was a military investigator, a court-appointed counsel and the statement was signed by Dr. Vesna Bosanac. And to go back to the very beginning I asked her about Ivica Nestorovic, the very soldier whose death Mrs. Bosanac is blamed for and accused of. She is here being accused of a war crime. Everything is linked up very closely. Everything is so closely knit. Djordje Kuzmanovic is a doctor whose existence Mrs. Bosanac confirms. He was there. It was based on his reports about the medical assistance provided to this soldier, namely that it was refused by Dr. Vesna Bosanac who, as the manager of the Vukovar medical centre, was in charge of all the minor medical stations throughout the town's area. In civil law, and I don't think there is a major discrepancy between common law and civil law in terms of how war crimes are viewed, and we are using a mixed system here, in a way, then we should be in a very good position to discuss these facts that may or may not affect the credibility of a witness being heard before this Tribunal. Therefore, since there are indications, and I've tried asking the witness about that, as to how she was exchanged -- may I continue? That means, I believed, this whole subject matter to be highly relevant, all the more so since this Trial Chamber and I certainly hope my learned friend and colleague, too, know full well that there is no statute of limitations on a war crime under no legal system in the world, and the person accused of a war crime cannot be exchanged. Why is the Defence bringing up a case like this? This is a fact that we must discuss during this trial. It is highly relevant also to the Trial Chamber when they make their decision. The fact is the reports on National Guards Corps presence, the police, the shelling, everything. We may be facing a person here whose credibility is in some way compromised. It is my duty and obligation to inform the Trial Chamber accordingly. It is my duty and obligation to question the witness on that count. And we shall not pass up our opportunity to examine these matters before the Chamber.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: Mr. Borovic, do we understand that it is the credibility of the witness upon which you focus?

utterances.speaker: MR. BOROVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] As I have said, this is the conclusion of my cross-examination, and, yes, I would like to focus on the credibility of the witness because we believe that she may be testifying -- testifying about the facts that she is not competent enough to testify about, and this is what we believe.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: So that you are advancing this document as indicating matters that may be adverse to the credit of this witness?

utterances.speaker: MR. BOROVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] The reason why I started this was to focus on the credibility but there is also a broader context. I cannot describe the entire context through this witness. But all of this is relevant because there is political influence not only whether it comes to trials but also when it comes to everything going on in Vukovar. I didn't ask her for no reason about whether she knew about Ustashas. The term "filthy Ustashas" was used very frequently.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: Mr. Borovic, you keep getting away. I'm not looking for the whole of your case. I'm trying to understand what it is about these documents that you see is immediately relevant. And as I understand it, the order for investigation you are advancing as relevant to the credit which the Chamber should attach to the evidence of this witness. Is that it? Do I correctly understand that?

utterances.speaker: MR. BOROVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you for your patience, Your Honours. The one you display both in relation to the Prosecution and Defence. It is important for the following reason. I will be very brief. If the Statute of limitation cannot run out on a war crime, if we know that the proceedings were suspended but not finalised, we know that this all goes to the credibility of this witness who is a person who was charged for having committed a war crime. The proceedings were never finalised and she was never acquitted. This is the gist of what I'm trying to say.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: Thank you. That's made that matter clear. The other two documents, what is the relevance of those?

utterances.speaker: MR. BOROVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honours, the first and the second document are the basis for the third document, which is the most important. Based on the first two documents, which contain facts about the crime for which the witness is charged, culminate in the final ruling on investigation. So in order not to put to her just the third document, in order to avoid any problems, I tendered the first two documents as well. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: Now, as I understand it, the third document is an order for investigation. Have there been formal charges? Is it your case that there are formal charges that have been laid?

utterances.speaker: MR. BOROVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honours, it is not your obligation to be familiar with the proceedings that were instituted at the time. However, all of this is formal and was done in accordance with the then-law of the SFRY on criminal procedure. The Prosecutor, the investigative judge, Defence counsel and the accused complied with all relevant provisions at the time. She signed the statement in B/C/S. The investigative Judge puts to the suspect the charges relevant in the case. Therefore, I think we are wasting our time for nothing. This is an official document, much more official than any of the faxes of which some were signed, some were not, and sent to -- we don't know exactly whom. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: Mr. Borovic, are you saying that there has not been any further formal charge beyond this order for investigation?

utterances.speaker: MR. BOROVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I apologise. I didn't quite understand. There can be just one act of accusation. It is not called "indictment" in our system. This is a decision to commence an investigation, which is issued after a preliminary investigation and, in the course of that, witnesses are questioned and facts are compiled, facts concerning the death of this witness -- of this soldier, and only after that is completed, the judge issues the decision to institute an official investigation. And then the Court issued a decision to suspend proceedings, therefore not to drop the charges but rather to suspend proceedings and then the witness was exchanged but that means that the proceedings are still in progress. The charges were not dropped and the statute of limitation does not run out on war crimes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: Are you saying that there is and will be no further form of charge than is contained in this document?

utterances.speaker: MR. BOROVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Dr. Bosanac is charged with armed rebellion as well. An investigation was conducted in relation to that crime as well. A larger number of crimes were investigated. At the time, Croatia was not internationally recognised, was not an independent state. Therefore, all of these decisions were legally valid at the time, including the ruling that we have here. Therefore, the crime of armed rebellion in which the witness participated at the time, together with the ZNG, and para-police forces, was detailed in all of these documents and in the criminal proceedings conducted at the time, and at the end, a ruling was issued stating that there are reasonable grounds to believe that the witness committed all of these acts based on which an official investigation ought to be instituted. So this is a formal state of affairs. I would like to ask the witness to refrain from laughing. Unlike the indictment we have here --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: Mr. Borovic, don't worry about the witness, if I can suggest. Very well, they, all three of them go to credit, and the credit, you say, is of significance because the witness may well be under investigation with -- of the possibility of herself having committed serious war crimes, and that may well influence and affect the nature of the evidence she is giving in this case. Is that the position?

utterances.speaker: MR. BOROVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] That's precisely so, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: Thank you. If I could now once again turn to Mr. Moore? Credit is said to be the relevance. Now, Mr. Moore, can you tell me whether you question the authenticity of the documents in the are in the sort of form that comes from the OTP. And the question is whether or not -- not all of them but at least the ruling, as I understand it.

utterances.speaker: MR. MOORE
utterances.text: I will try and not give evidence. The statements that I have seen are not OTP documents.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: Are they not? Right.

utterances.speaker: MR. MOORE
utterances.text: But can I just say there is over 900 documents and I can't honestly put my hand on heart to say they are not OTP documents but I believe they are not. My -- the second matter is my learned friend has - I don't mean to be unkind - given evidence in relation to the procedure. But as far as I understand there has been no formal charge - I'm having that matter checked now - and I submit that that is an important criteria, with regard to the documents. Answering your question, I do not know if they are valid or not.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: Very well.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: Mr. Borovic, the Court at the moment would propose to admit these three documents only as marked for identification. The question of their authenticity is at issue, and it will be necessary for you, if you want to pursue them into evidence as exhibits, to deal with the question of their authenticity, either by persuading Mr. Moore in discussions that they are authentic or by establishing their authenticity in due course. On their face at the moment, we don't see that sufficiently established. Nor is it clear to us, for example, whether the document which is the investigation order and ruling is one that was made in -- on the 4th or some date in May of 2000, or, as you say, in 1992, because what is on it doesn't give that date at all but only gives one in 2000. So each of these documents will now be received only as marked for identification.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOROVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honours, I naturally cannot question your rulings. I accept them. I would like to point out that the Prosecutor interrupted me when I started questioning the witness about this JNA soldier, when she said that she heard about him. I was about to put additional questions in order to reach the whole point. If she heard this in the military court --

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] No. I didn't hear it in the military court, but in the prison when I was investigated.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOROVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. BOROVIC
utterances.text: No need to go into that because the Court has ruled.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOROVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] All right. I'm not going to comment on your ruling, and I will be able to prove all of these things later on, and this will be admitted in the evidence, I believe. There is another document that I wanted to tender, 2D01.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: And the Court officer will now give these documents their identification number.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honour. The report signed by m Major General Mile Babic, that will be Exhibit marked for identification number 00041. The official note of the provisional secretariat of interior will be identified as number 42. And the ruling of the military court in Belgrade will be identified as number 43, marked for identification.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: Now, Mr. Borovic, you were going on to some other matter?

utterances.speaker: MR. BOROVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I will have just one more question, but prior to that, yesterday I tendered into evidence reports we received, or rather a decision to remove from office issued by the Ministry of Health under number 2D 01-0001. This is the decision -- this is the document discussed yesterday, both by the Prosecution and Defence, and I believe that the time is ripe now for it to be tendered.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: Is this the document at your tab 1?

utterances.speaker: MR. BOROVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] That's right.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: Any objection, Mr. Moore?

utterances.speaker: MR. MOORE
utterances.text: No objection.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: It will be received as an exhibit.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honour. It will be Exhibit number 44.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: Now, was there any other document, Mr. Borovic, or is that the end of the documents?

utterances.speaker: MR. BOROVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] No.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: Thank you. Now, were there any other questions?

utterances.speaker: MR. BOROVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I think perhaps two.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: Two?

utterances.speaker: MR. BOROVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Two.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: Go ahead now.

utterances.speaker: MR. MOORE
utterances.text: Your Honour, may I just make one small inquiry of my learned friend via the Court? And it is this: That he has already said that there is a document that was signed by Dr. Bosanac at these hearings. I don't know if in actual fact it is the intention for the doctor to be shown that document and to confirm whether it is her signature or not. I would not wish that document to come in later on in the trial without it having been confirmed that it is her signature or not.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOROVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Does this have to do only with the issue of the signature or perhaps some other issues that I could put to the witness? But at any rate, I do not believe that it will come up later as something that Dr. Vesna Bosanac has to comment upon that, because there are other pieces of evidence that later on we should be able to tender. Therefore, we will not be showing any document to this witness now, nor did I propose any other document.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: Thank you. Well, you are on notice of Mr. Moore's point. You had two questions.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOROVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] That's what I said.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOROVIC
utterances.text: The first question: Do you know that members of the National Guards Corps were called Ustashas by their opponents in this military conflict?

utterances.speaker: VESNA BOSANAC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, I'm not aware much that.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOROVIC
utterances.text: You never heard that?

utterances.speaker: VESNA BOSANAC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No. Except what I have previously stated, that one of the passengers in the car asked whether those were Ustashas.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOROVIC
utterances.text: And if I may ask, were you ever a member of the Communist Party?

utterances.speaker: VESNA BOSANAC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I became a member of the Communist League, the youth section, but I was never a communist by conviction.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOROVIC
utterances.text: So what's the difference between becoming a member and not actually being a communist?

utterances.speaker: VESNA BOSANAC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I was proposed for membership and accepted into the Communist Party, and actually being a communist means being actively involved in the activities of the party.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOROVIC
utterances.text: A subquestion to my previous question: When you applied for your position, did you have to declare your political -- your political affiliations?

utterances.speaker: VESNA BOSANAC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I can't remember.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOROVIC
utterances.text: At that time, it was mandatory to declare yourself politically. I think everybody was a communist in Croatia back then.

utterances.speaker: VESNA BOSANAC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't think you're right on that point but I really couldn't say.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOROVIC
utterances.text: Thank you very much.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOROVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] No further questions.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. Borovic. We will take a break now and resume at quarter past 12.00 -- quarter past 1.00. --- Break taken at 12.53 p.m.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. Lukic?

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honours, on account of our changes in schedule, shall we stop at quarter to 2 or shall we press on? I need to know this in order to be able to formulate our questions.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: There is another hearing to follow us in this courtroom.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Mrs. Bosanac, good afternoon to you.

utterances.speaker: VESNA BOSANAC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Good afternoon.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: My name is Novak Lukic. I'm an attorney at law from Belgrade. I will ask you a number of questions on behalf of Veselin Sljivancanin' defence team. Before I start with my questions, I wish to inform you that there are certain issues about which I will try to refresh your memory, the expression we use in legalese, especially as concerns your contact with my client. I will try to inform you about his position regarding some of your statements and claims which you will then be at liberty to confirm or deny based on your own information concerning certain evens. I will try to phrase my questions in such a way that you would be able to answer briefly, mostly yes or no questions. If there are further clarifications you feel you need to provide, the Prosecutor can clarify matters with you on re-examination. First of all, I would like to ask you a number of questions about the October evacuation that you spoke about. You said that the October evacuation, on October 1991, had been organised by an organisation known as Medecins Sans Frontieres, doctors without frontiers; is that right?

utterances.speaker: VESNA BOSANAC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Does the name Michel Robert mean anything to you?

utterances.speaker: VESNA BOSANAC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I can remember that name.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: For the sake of the transcript, I said Michel Robert. Do you have any information that this person or someone else escorting the convoy on behalf of that organisation, changed the route previously suggested by the JNA of their own accord? Do you have any information concerning that?

utterances.speaker: VESNA BOSANAC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: At this point in time, and we are talking about October 1991, was the JNA able to offer anyone guarantees of a safe passage through the village of Bogdanovci?

utterances.speaker: VESNA BOSANAC [Resumed]
utterances.text: You mean the time the convoy took place?

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Yes, I mean October.

utterances.speaker: VESNA BOSANAC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. I think they were able to.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: It is your submission that the village of Bogdanovci was under JNA control at the time in its entirety?

utterances.speaker: VESNA BOSANAC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, I think so but I'm not quite certain. In early October, at least based on the information that I had, the JNA took over Bogdanovci in its entirety. But I can't give you exact date.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Are you familiar with the fact that the vehicle with two Swiss nurses from Switzerland were wounded, that was part of the convoy when it came across a minefield, that specific piece of territory was under the control of the Croatian forces? Is this something you know?

utterances.speaker: VESNA BOSANAC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No. I'm not sure about the exact spot where this incident occurred.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Thank you. Do you know that those nurses were then offered medical assistance at the military medical academy in Belgrade?

utterances.speaker: VESNA BOSANAC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, I didn't know that.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: On the 25th of October, I think that was the first day of your testimony, which is when you addressed there subject, on page 33 of the transcript, you said that the convoy was supposed to transport Croatian soldiers and wounded civilians for treatment. Do you remember that you said that?

utterances.speaker: VESNA BOSANAC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Who decided on behalf of the medical personnel of the hospital who would be joining the convoy?

utterances.speaker: VESNA BOSANAC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Dr. Njavro and his associates. He set the priorities in terms of who would be allowed to go in order to receive further treatment.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Do you know that a soldier was forced to join the convoy against his free will, a man named Ivan Zivkovic who was being treated at the hospital at the time. Do you know anything about that?

utterances.speaker: VESNA BOSANAC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No. I've been asked about that already. I know nothing about that.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Did you later hear that he called out for help to JNA soldiers from the convoy, yelling that he was there against his free will and asking them to release him from this convoy en route for Zagreb? Do you know anything about that?

utterances.speaker: VESNA BOSANAC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Today, when answering questions by my colleague Mr. Borovic in relation to the ceasing of the shelling of the hospital, you said something that is not consistent with your statement from 1995 when you said that the shelling stopped on the 17th, whereas today you said there were still shells falling in the hospital yard or around the hospital on the 18th. Isn't that correct?

utterances.speaker: VESNA BOSANAC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: I've been following the transcripts from other trials at this Tribunal. Correct me if I'm wrong, please. You keep claiming that this was an aggression and not a conflict. You said so in the Milosevic trial. Is that your submission to this Chamber?

utterances.speaker: VESNA BOSANAC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Do you know that Vukovar was shelled from the direction of Vinkovci by the Croatian army? Is this something that you're familiar with, yes or no?

utterances.speaker: VESNA BOSANAC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Do you know that when the Vrazdin Corps was surrendered prior to the Vukovar operation the Croatian army had obtained a huge amount of heavy weaponry which was subsequently transferred to Vinkovci?

utterances.speaker: VESNA BOSANAC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, I don't know about that.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Were you ever interested in how many JNA soldiers were killed during this operation? Are you familiar with the specific figures or did you ever want to know?

utterances.speaker: VESNA BOSANAC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I heard something but informally. I certainly would like to know but I do not have the information.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: If I told you that my information was that during the clashes, the JNA suffered over 1.100 casualties, would you tend to agree with that?

utterances.speaker: VESNA BOSANAC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I really can't say anything about that. I simply don't know.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: What do you think killed those people, regardless of their exact numbers, as a medical worker? What do you think?

utterances.speaker: VESNA BOSANAC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't know.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: I assume that you were in touch in some way with Mr. Dedakovic for as long as he was present in or around the town. He was the commander of Vukovar's defence, right?

utterances.speaker: VESNA BOSANAC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Did he personally or anyone else ever inform you of their conversations with my client, Mr. Sljivancanin, via radio link whether they talked about Mr. Sljivancanin's desire for the Croatian Army to surrender so that the destruction of the town might be stopped? Do you know anything about that?

utterances.speaker: VESNA BOSANAC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Mrs. Bosanac, do you have any direct, personal knowledge, did anyone tell you, perhaps, that in the last days of war operations in Vukovar, the 17th and the 18th, there is a certain amount of confusion about the specific date, namely that rather large number of ZNG members tried to break through Luzac, which was under the control of the Croatian forces, and many of those who failed to achieve a breakthrough returned to the centre of town specifically to the hospital? I have a number of questions about this. Please tell me whatever you know.

utterances.speaker: VESNA BOSANAC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I know that they were trying to organise a breakthrough for several days. I know about that week, around the 17th, when my son was involved in one of those attempts at a breakthrough. I also know that some of them were killed in these attempts. Some were captured. I don't know who came back eventually or where they went to.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Can we please go into private session briefly?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: Private session.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: We are in open session, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation].

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: In your testimony, you said that you spent the night between the 19th and the 20th in Negoslavci; is that right?

utterances.speaker: VESNA BOSANAC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: What about the next day, when you returned to the hospital, or later on, generally speaking? Did you ever hear that on the evening of the 19th, four JNA soldiers were killed by mines in the vicinity of the hospital? Did you hear anything about an incident like that?

utterances.speaker: VESNA BOSANAC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Yesterday or rather the day before yesterday, on the 26th, in answer to a question by the Prosecutor about whether you knew whether the hospital was being used for non-medical purposes, on page 27 you said that you were spending all your days at the hospital and then certainly you would have known had the hospital been used for any other purposes but medical. Isn't that what you said?

utterances.speaker: VESNA BOSANAC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: I assume you did not spend all of your time sitting in your office. You must have been able to move about the hospital, inspect the situation, see for yourself what was going on?

utterances.speaker: VESNA BOSANAC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Furthermore, I assume that as hospital manager you took an active part on what the rules of behaviour would be in those days inside the hospital?

utterances.speaker: VESNA BOSANAC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: I'm putting it to you, Mrs. Bosanac, that you were fully informed about the fact that members of the ZNG were in fact in the hospital on those last days trying to change clothes and dress as civilians and medical staff in order to conceal their true identities. Would I be mistaken in saying that?

utterances.speaker: VESNA BOSANAC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, you would be mistaken.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Do you know who Tomic Jozo is?

utterances.speaker: VESNA BOSANAC [Resumed]
utterances.text: You mean the doctor?

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: That's precisely my question. Who was Jozo Tomic? What did he do?

utterances.speaker: VESNA BOSANAC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Dr. Jozo Tomic was a general practitioner, a physician. He had just begun his residence with the gynaecology ward, but then he was called up for military service and in September 1991 he returned to Vukovar. He worked with the emergency unit at the Vukovar Hospital.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: To the very last day, right?

utterances.speaker: VESNA BOSANAC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Was he one of the doctors who were in charge of drawing up lists of wounded? Do you know anything about that?

utterances.speaker: VESNA BOSANAC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. He was one of them. All of the doctors who were treating the wounded had to produce lists. Dr. Matos and Dr. Tomic made lists of patients who just came in in order to have their wounds dressed. Outpatients in other words.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Do you know that he personally placed people on these lists who were in fact not wounded at the time? Do you know anything about that?

utterances.speaker: VESNA BOSANAC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Prior to this, I asked you about a person in a private session. I done want to repeat the name now. But would it mean anything to you if I were to tell you that one of these three persons asked this doctor to place them on the list of wounded even though he was not wounded? Did you ever speak to Dr. Tomic about that?

utterances.speaker: VESNA BOSANAC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Mrs. Bosanac, would you approve someone's name being put on the list of wounded or would you approve camouflaging somebody as a patient if that person wasn't that? Would you approve that?

utterances.speaker: VESNA BOSANAC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Does the name Mihalj Kolesar mean anything to you?

utterances.speaker: VESNA BOSANAC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I think he's the husband of Mrs. Kolesar; is that right?

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: I was unable to establish that based on the statement I received.

utterances.speaker: VESNA BOSANAC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I'm not sure about that.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: The person in this case was born in 1935 and, according to his statement, he was at the hospital from October on, helping there. His wife worked at the hospital.

utterances.speaker: VESNA BOSANAC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. Then that's probably the same person.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Did you have -- did you ever have a conflict with there person?

utterances.speaker: VESNA BOSANAC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: If I were to tell you that he stated to the OTP that it was you who said that everybody should put white coats on when the wounded were taken out, do you think that he had any reasons to lie?

utterances.speaker: VESNA BOSANAC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't know whether he had any reasons to lie but I never stated anything like that, and I don't know that he ever testified. Perhaps we are not referring to the same person.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: At any rate, it is your evidence that you never told anybody to put on white coats; is that right?

utterances.speaker: VESNA BOSANAC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Yesterday we looked at your list, or rather the list from the indictment marked by you. As far as I understood, and you can correct me if I'm wrong, it is your evidence that all of those marked with an "S" indicating -- denoting soldier, were members of the ZNG who were actually wounded, is that your evidence?

utterances.speaker: VESNA BOSANAC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No. Some were wounded. Some of those marked with an "S." But there were also persons I marked as help workers, and soldiers who were at the hospital as part of security detail, and as part of help workers and who were actually policemen or soldiers.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: So in that list of yours, you treat them as help workers?

utterances.speaker: VESNA BOSANAC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: So you are trying to say that among the people killed in Ovcara, there were no?

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Could the counsel please repeat his question?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] [No interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation].

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Those whom you marked with an "S," marking them as soldiers, were all of them ill? Were all of them wounded?

utterances.speaker: VESNA BOSANAC [Resumed]
utterances.text: According to my information, yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Do you know that among the bodies in Ovcara that you are aware of, and who have been identified, do you know whether there was a single person among them who was a policeman or a soldier, without being wounded, without being a medical worker, without being a civilian?

utterances.speaker: VESNA BOSANAC [Resumed]
utterances.text: What do you mean a single person?

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Well, do you know of any?

utterances.speaker: VESNA BOSANAC [Resumed]
utterances.text: As I have stated previously, I have the accurate list of persons identified so far from the mass grave in Ovcara. The list that we have here states that those were the missing persons. In addition to that, I also have a list of the wounded who were wounded and identified in Ovcara.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: However, you did not answer my question, and I will repeat it. Among the persons whom according to you, you knew before the events in Ovcara, do you remember whether among them there were any policemen or soldiers? Yes or no?

utterances.speaker: VESNA BOSANAC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I can't answer your question specifically. Please tell me who do you have in mind specifically? If you have somebody in mind.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: In your list, you categorised people into several categories. Those people whom you knew. You didn't mark any of them as soldiers?

utterances.speaker: VESNA BOSANAC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, I did. I marked them with an "S."

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Well, let's clarify this. So in this "S" category, were all of the people in that category wounded?

utterances.speaker: VESNA BOSANAC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Those whom I knew, yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Do you know that in relation to this statement, even the OTP does not believe you? Have you actually read the indictment? Because it's a public document.

utterances.speaker: VESNA BOSANAC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, I haven't.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: The OTP claims that among the persons listed in paragraph 32, they were -- some of them were active soldiers, are you aware of that?

utterances.speaker: VESNA BOSANAC [Resumed]
utterances.text: What are you trying to ask me here? I have not read the indictment, not officially.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: All right. I was just trying to establish your credibility, and it is not your duty to be familiar with the indictment. I would like to briefly touch upon another topic. I hope to conclude before we adjourn. It has to do with the number of the ill, wounded and those who went missing later on who were at the hospital and were supposed to be evacuated. I will put several questions to you in relation to your appeals. We spent almost an entire day going over them, and in terms of their content these appeals were quite dramatic. Mrs. Bosanac, would you agree with me that, ultimately, you did manipulate with the number of the wounded when sending those appeals, yes or no?

utterances.speaker: VESNA BOSANAC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: I think you stated yesterday, but I can't be certain of it, that the information on the number of the wounded was sent by you on a daily basis to the Ministry of Health and some of that information was transmitted by MUP?

utterances.speaker: VESNA BOSANAC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: You also said that from the 18th on, no new wounded arrived in the hospital, or rather no new names were registered; is that right?

utterances.speaker: VESNA BOSANAC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Please tell us, the lists you forwarded to the Ministry of Health on a daily basis, upon your arrival in Zagreb, did you have occasion to see them, yes or no?

utterances.speaker: VESNA BOSANAC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Some of them, yes, some no. I saw the database that we continuously entered into the computer, and then sent via e-mail.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: We would like to know what kind of electronic communication existed in 1991?

utterances.speaker: VESNA BOSANAC [Resumed]
utterances.text: The one that I'm describing to you. I don't know what you are expecting of me.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: And why is it that you didn't send your appeals via electronic mail?

utterances.speaker: VESNA BOSANAC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Because I couldn't. As I told you, the computer was pre-programmed and we used it to enter data into it.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: And then you forwarded it by electronic mail?

utterances.speaker: VESNA BOSANAC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honours, I have some documents to put to the witness and I think it would be more appropriate if we did that on Monday.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. Lukic. We must now adjourn. I'm sorry that we have not been able to conclude your evidence there week, doctor. We resume on Monday, and it is in the afternoon next week. This will be the first time that counsel and accused have encountered the sittings that run until 7.00 at night in this trial. We start at 2.15 and go until 7.00. On the first day, Monday, we will break earlier, which may help people to adjust into that programme. We will break, I think, at a convenient time between 6.15 and 6.30, but you will understand that we will have to get into the pattern of finishing at 7.00 if we are to keep the pace of the trial working. In the weeks that follow, for most of November and December, we seem to be alternating weeks, mornings one week, afternoons the next week. So I hope you will all be able to adjust to that work pattern. We will now adjourn and resume at 2.15 on Monday.
